Foods that start with the letter K.Kale: Once the garnish of salad bars, this leafy green became a superfood star in the 2010s; it was a common food in medieval Europe long before.
Foods that start with the letter K.Kiwi: Kiwifruit is native to China, and was renamed in New Zealand in the 1950s after the country's flightless bird, which also has fuzzy brown coloring.
Foods that start with the letter K.Kimchi: Korea's fermented vegetable dish, usually napa cabbage with chili, comes in hundreds of varieties, and families once buried it in clay pots for winter.
Foods that start with the letter K.Kebab: The word comes from Persian and Arabic roots for roasted meat, and in Turkey the döner kebab is carved from a vertical rotating spit.
Foods that start with the letter K.Ketchup: The name likely comes from a Chinese fermented fish sauce, and tomatoes only joined the recipe in the early 1800s, so early ketchups used mushrooms or walnuts.
Foods that start with the letter K.Kumquat: This tiny citrus is eaten whole: the peel is sweet and the flesh tart, the opposite of an orange, and the name means golden orange in Cantonese.
Foods that start with the letter K.Kohlrabi: The name means cabbage turnip in German, and the round, crunchy part is actually a swollen stem, not a root, and it tastes like mild broccoli.
Foods that start with the letter K.Kidney bean: It is named for its shape and color, and raw kidney beans are toxic: just a few undercooked ones can cause severe stomach illness, so they must be boiled.
Foods that start with the letter K.Kombucha: This fizzy fermented tea is made with a SCOBY, a symbiotic culture of bacteria and yeast, which forms a floating rubbery disc.
Foods that start with the letter K.Kielbasa: Polish for sausage, and in Poland it covers many kinds; in the US the word usually means a smoked, garlicky pork sausage.
Foods that start with the letter K.Kefir: A tangy fermented milk drink made with grains that are not cereal but a clump of bacteria and yeast, and it originated in the Caucasus mountains.
Foods that start with the letter K.Kipper: A whole herring split, salted and cold-smoked, it is a traditional British breakfast, especially from the Isle of Man and Craster in Northumberland.
Foods that start with the letter K.Cabbage: A trap: it sounds like a K word because of kale and kohlrabi relatives, but it starts with C; ancient Romans considered it a hangover cure.
Foods that start with the letter K.Carrot: The C is a trap, since it sounds like K; the carrot was originally purple or white, and the orange variety was bred in the Netherlands.
Foods that start with the letter K.Cucumber: It begins with C despite the K sound at the start; cucumbers are about 95 percent water and are actually a fruit, botanically.
Foods that start with the letter K.Cauliflower: It starts with a C that sounds like K; Mark Twain called it nothing but cabbage with a college education.
Foods that start with the letter K.Corn: Corn sounds like it starts with K but is spelled with a C; its kernels are fruits, each silk strand leading to a single kernel.
Foods that start with the letter K.Quiche: Quiche is pronounced keesh, so it sounds like a K food, but the spelling starts with Q; it originated in Lorraine in northeastern France.
Foods that start with the letter K.Quinoa: Pronounced keen-wah, it sounds like a K food but starts with Q; the Incas called it the mother grain and it is actually a seed.
Foods that start with the letter K.Couscous: It sounds like it starts with K, but spelled with a C; couscous is tiny steamed balls of semolina pasta, and a North African staple.
Foods that start with the letter K.Cashew: Another hard C, not a K: cashews grow hanging from the bottom of a cashew apple, and their shells contain a caustic oil related to poison ivy.
Foods that start with the letter K.Clam: It starts with C, and the sound is a K, so it looks like a K but is not; some ocean quahog clams have lived more than 500 years.
Foods that start with the letter K.Coconut: It sounds like a K word with its hard C; the coconut is not really a nut but a drupe, and can float across oceans to colonize islands.
Foods that start with the letter K.Croissant: It begins with a C and a K sound in French; the crescent pastry is Austrian in origin, a version of the kipferl, and became French in the 1800s.

Japanese sweets.Mochi: Glutinous rice is pounded into a stretchy cake; it is a New Year tradition, and every year a few people choke on it.
Japanese sweets.Dorayaki: Two fluffy pancakes sandwiching sweet red bean paste, famously the favorite snack of the manga robot cat Doraemon.
Japanese sweets.Taiyaki: Fish-shaped cakes, typically filled with red bean paste, are baked in a mold; 'tai' is sea bream, a lucky fish.
Japanese sweets.Dango: Chewy rice-flour dumplings on a skewer, often glazed with sweet soy; they're eaten at moon-viewing festivals.
Japanese sweets.Daifuku: Its name means 'great luck': a soft mochi wrapper around sweet bean paste, with strawberry-filled ichigo daifuku a modern hit.
Japanese sweets.Yokan: A firm jelly of red bean paste and agar sliced like a bar, served with green tea for centuries.
Japanese sweets.Castella: This honey-rich sponge cake came to Nagasaki with Portuguese traders in the 1500s, and the name may come from Castile.
Japanese sweets.Melonpan: This sweet bun gets its name from its melon-like crosshatch crust, and usually contains no melon at all.
Japanese sweets.Kakigori: Finely shaved ice drizzled with syrup, a summer treat in Japan dating back to the Heian period, when nobles ate it.
Japanese sweets.Monaka: Sweet bean paste sandwiched between crisp wafers made from mochi rice; it's a classic gift sweet.
Japanese sweets.Manju: Steamed buns of sweet red bean paste, thought to have come from China with a monk in the 14th century.
Japanese sweets.Bingsu: Korean shaved ice, topped with red beans, fruit, or condensed milk, is a Korean dessert, and not a Japanese sweet.
Japanese sweets.Hotteok: Korean sweet pancakes filled with brown sugar and nuts, a winter street food, not Japanese.
Japanese sweets.Mooncake: A rich, dense Chinese pastry for the Mid-Autumn Festival, so it's not Japanese.
Japanese sweets.Egg tart: Flaky pastry holding a glossy custard filling, popular in Hong Kong, derived from the Portuguese, and not Japanese.
Japanese sweets.Baklava: A Middle Eastern layered pastry, with nuts and syrup.
Japanese sweets.Churros: Fried dough sticks from Spain and Latin America; not Japanese.
Japanese sweets.Halo-halo: A Filipino dessert whose name means 'mix-mix', a sundae of shaved ice, beans, jellies and ice cream.
Japanese sweets.Gulab jamun: Syrup-soaked milk dumplings, an Indian sweet.
Japanese sweets.Macaron: A French almond meringue sandwich cookie, not to be mistaken for coconut macaroons.
Japanese sweets.Tiramisu: Italian coffee-and-mascarpone dessert, whose name means 'pick me up'.
Japanese sweets.Kulfi: Indian dense ice cream made without churning.
Japanese sweets.Tteok: The general term for Korean rice cakes, which resemble mochi but are Korean.
Japanese sweets.Pastel de nata: Portugal's custard tart, which also gave Asian egg tarts their start; it is Portuguese, not Japanese.

Food that grows underground.Peanut: Peanuts are legumes, not nuts, and the flower stalk bends down to push the pods under the soil to ripen.
Food that grows underground.Cassava: Cassava is a starchy root that feeds hundreds of millions of people in the tropics, and must be processed to remove natural cyanide.
Food that grows underground.Truffle: Truffles are fungi that grow underground near tree roots, and pigs or trained dogs are used to sniff them out.
Food that grows underground.Cashew: Cashews grow outside the fruit, hanging from a cashew apple on a tree, and the shell contains an irritating oil.
Food that grows underground.Almond: Almonds are seeds of a tree fruit related to peaches, and they grow on branches, not underground.
Food that grows underground.Walnut: Walnuts fall from trees in a green husk, and the nuts grow above ground.
Food that grows underground.Tomato: Tomatoes grow above ground on vines and are botanically fruits.
Food that grows underground.Broccoli: Broccoli forms its flowering heads above the soil, so we eat the buds, not the roots.
Food that grows underground.Pumpkin: Pumpkins grow along the ground on vines, but sit on the surface, not under it.
Food that grows underground.Pea: Peas grow in pods on climbing vines, well above the ground.
Food that grows underground.Corn: Corn grows on tall stalks, with each ear holding hundreds of kernels, and each silk thread leads to one kernel.
Food that grows underground.Celery: Celery grows upward, and its stalks are leaf stalks, mostly above ground.
Food that grows underground.Cabbage: Cabbages sit above ground as tightly packed heads of leaves.
Food that grows underground.Pineapple: Pineapples grow on top of a short, spiky plant above ground, and not under it.

Animals that live in trees.Sloth: A sloth's slow metabolism means it comes down from the tree to the ground only about once a week to go to the toilet.
Animals that live in trees.Orangutan: The name means person of the forest, and these apes build a fresh sleeping nest in the trees every night.
Animals that live in trees.Tree frog: Sticky toe pads, and often bright green skin, let tree frogs cling to leaves, and some never touch the ground.
Animals that live in trees.Spider monkey: Its prehensile tail works like a fifth hand, strong enough to support its entire weight.
Animals that live in trees.Tree kangaroo: Unlike its ground cousins, this New Guinea relative climbs trees, and can leap down 15 meters unharmed.
Animals that live in trees.Gibbon: Gibbons swing arm over arm, a style called brachiation, and can cover about 15 meters in a single leap.
Animals that live in trees.Red panda: A red panda isn't closely related to the giant panda, and it uses its bushy tail like a blanket.
Animals that live in trees.Tarsier: Each eye of this tiny primate is as big as its brain, and it can rotate its head nearly 180 degrees.
Animals that live in trees.Flying squirrel: It doesn't truly fly, but glides by stretching a skin flap between its limbs, sometimes for over 50 meters.
Animals that live in trees.Green tree python: Newborns are yellow or red and turn green as they mature, and it sleeps coiled over a branch.
Animals that live in trees.Kangaroo: Kangaroos hop on powerful hind legs across open ground, and they can't walk backward.
Animals that live in trees.Meerkat: Meerkats live in burrows in Africa's dry plains, not trees.
Animals that live in trees.Hippo: A hippo spends the day in water, then walks on land at night to graze, but never climbs trees.
Animals that live in trees.Zebra: Each zebra's stripe pattern is unique, and zebras live on open grasslands, not in trees.
Animals that live in trees.Mole: Moles spend their lives in underground tunnels, nearly blind, and are the opposite of tree dwellers.
Animals that live in trees.Ostrich: The largest living bird can't fly or climb, but it can run about 70 kilometers an hour.
Animals that live in trees.Penguin: Penguins are flightless birds that swim, and they never nest in trees.
Animals that live in trees.Armadillo: A ground-dwelling, armored animal that digs for insects, and it can't climb trees.
Animals that live in trees.Badger: Badgers live in underground setts, not in trees, and they dig more than they climb.
Animals that live in trees.Hedgehog: Hedgehogs nest in leaf piles and hedges on the ground, and they roll into a spiky ball.
Animals that live in trees.Wombat: A wombat is a burrowing marsupial, not a tree climber, and its pouch faces backward so it doesn't fill with dirt.
Animals that live in trees.Camel: Camels walk in desert land and store fat, not water, in their humps.
Animals that live in trees.Bison: The heaviest land animal in North America lives on grasslands and is far too heavy to climb.

Animals that truly fly (not just glide).Bat: Bats are the only mammals capable of true, powered flight. Their wings are webbed hands, and they make up about a fifth of all mammal species.
Animals that truly fly (not just glide).Bee: Honeybees beat their wings about 230 times a second, which creates the buzz. A bee can fly at roughly 25 km/h.
Animals that truly fly (not just glide).Butterfly: Butterflies fly with scale-covered wings. Some, like the monarch, migrate up to about 4,000 km, over generations.
Animals that truly fly (not just glide).Dragonfly: Dragonflies flap each of their four wings independently, so they can hover, fly backwards, and even mate in flight. They've existed for over 300 million years.
Animals that truly fly (not just glide).Moth: Moths are mostly night fliers and navigate partly by moonlight. Lights confuse them, which may be why they circle lamps.
Animals that truly fly (not just glide).Ladybug: Ladybugs are beetles, so they have a hard wing case, with delicate flying wings folded underneath. They hibernate in clusters.
Animals that truly fly (not just glide).Mosquito: Mosquitoes beat their wings up to hundreds of times per second, making that whine. Only the females bite, as they need blood protein for eggs.
Animals that truly fly (not just glide).Hummingbird: Hummingbirds can hover and even fly backwards, beating their wings up to about 80 times per second. They're the smallest birds.
Animals that truly fly (not just glide).Eagle: Eagles soar on thermals with wingspans over two metres. Their eyesight is several times sharper than a human's.
Animals that truly fly (not just glide).Pigeon: Pigeons fly at speeds of over 80 km/h and can find home from hundreds of kilometres away. They were once used to carry military messages.
Animals that truly fly (not just glide).Housefly: Houseflies beat their wings around 200 times a second. They taste with their feet, and can land on ceilings by rolling upside-down.
Animals that truly fly (not just glide).Flying squirrel: Flying squirrels glide on a skin membrane, but can't flap to gain height. They can glide for distances of about 45 metres.
Animals that truly fly (not just glide).Flying fish: Flying fish launch from the water and glide, sometimes for 200 metres or more. They don't flap, so they glide rather than fly.
Animals that truly fly (not just glide).Sugar glider: Sugar gliders are small marsupials that glide between trees on skin flaps. They glide, but can't power themselves upward.
Animals that truly fly (not just glide).Colugo: Colugos, the 'flying lemurs', are neither lemurs nor flyers. They glide up to about 70 metres using the largest gliding membrane of any mammal.
Animals that truly fly (not just glide).Flying snake: Flying snakes of Southeast Asia flatten their bodies and ripple through the air to glide between trees. It's a glide, not flight.
Animals that truly fly (not just glide).Flying frog: Some tree frogs glide on enormous webbed feet. Wallace's flying frog can make controlled glides, but it can't truly fly.
Animals that truly fly (not just glide).Ostrich: The ostrich is a bird that can't fly, but it can run extremely fast. A single kick can seriously injure a predator.
Animals that truly fly (not just glide).Penguin: Penguins have wings, but they are flippers, used to 'fly' underwater. Emperor penguins can dive deeper than 500 metres.
Animals that truly fly (not just glide).Kiwi: Kiwis are flightless, with tiny vestigial wings hidden under their shaggy feathers. Their nostrils sit at the beak's tip, for sniffing out worms.
Animals that truly fly (not just glide).Emu: Emus have wings so small they're nearly invisible, and can't fly. They can still run at about 50 km/h.
Animals that truly fly (not just glide).Cassowary: The cassowary can't fly but has a bony casque on its head. Its dagger-like inner claw can reach about 12 cm long.
Animals that truly fly (not just glide).Draco lizard: Draco lizards glide using ribs that extend into wing-like flaps. They can travel about 60 metres between trees, but don't flap.
Animals that truly fly (not just glide).Rhea: Rheas are flightless South American birds who use their wings for balance when running and turning.

Shellfish.Shrimp: Its name is often used for several species, and the prawn and shrimp distinction is mostly a matter of regional naming.
Shellfish.Lobster: Lobsters are red after cooking because heat releases the red pigment astaxanthin, which is masked by proteins when alive.
Shellfish.Crab: King crabs are actually closer relatives of hermit crabs than of true crabs.
Shellfish.Oyster: A single oyster can filter many gallons of water a day, which makes oyster reefs natural water cleaners.
Shellfish.Mussel: Mussels cling to rocks with strong byssus threads, which cooks call the beard and remove.
Shellfish.Clam: A quahog clam nicknamed Ming was found off Iceland and lived about 500 years, the oldest animal known.
Shellfish.Scallop: It swims by clapping its shells, and can have up to 200 tiny eyes along its edge.
Shellfish.Crayfish: Called crawdads or mudbugs in the American South, they star in Louisiana boils.
Shellfish.Langoustine: Also called Norway lobster, it's the true source of what's served as scampi in many places.
Shellfish.Cockle: Cockles and mussels are famous from the song about Molly Malone, who sold them in Dublin.
Shellfish.Prawn: Prawn and shrimp have no clear scientific line, and countries use the words differently.
Shellfish.Whelk: These big sea snails are eaten in Britain, and their egg cases wash up on beaches as 'sea wash balls'.
Shellfish.Abalone: A sea snail with a shiny mother-of-pearl shell, its muscular foot is a prized delicacy in Chinese and Japanese cooking.
Shellfish.Salmon: It's a finfish, not a shellfish. Its pink flesh comes from astaxanthin, the same pigment that colors shrimp.
Shellfish.Tuna: A fast ocean fish with red flesh, not a shellfish. Some bluefin sell for huge prices at Tokyo auctions.
Shellfish.Cod: Cod is a finfish, once so abundant that its trade shaped New England; so not a shellfish.
Shellfish.Eel: Eels are fish. They spawn in the Sargasso Sea, a mystery that long puzzled scientists.
Shellfish.Anchovy: These tiny salty fish are the secret behind Caesar dressing and Worcestershire sauce, but they have scales, not shells.
Shellfish.Sardine: A fish, not a shellfish, though it's an oily one rich in omega-3s. The island Sardinia gave its name.
Shellfish.Swordfish: This fish has a sword-like bill, but it's a finfish.
Shellfish.Monkfish: A strange-looking, ugly fish, with a tail that tastes a bit like lobster, but still a finfish.
Shellfish.Halibut: A big flatfish, not shellfish, with both eyes migrating to the same side of its head as it grows.
Shellfish.Catfish: A freshwater fish with whisker-like barbels, a Southern US favorite, not shellfish.
Shellfish.Mackerel: A fish, not a shellfish, which is oily and fast and swims in huge schools.

National capitals in Europe.Madrid: Spain's capital is Europe's highest, at about 650 m above sea level. It became the capital in 1561.
National capitals in Europe.Rome: The Italian capital contains an entire country, the Vatican, and the Colosseum once held tens of thousands of spectators.
National capitals in Europe.Lisbon: Portugal's capital is among Europe's oldest, older than Rome by legend. A 1755 earthquake almost destroyed it.
National capitals in Europe.Vienna: The Austrian capital, once the heart of the Habsburg Empire. Its coffeehouse culture is on UNESCO's heritage list.
National capitals in Europe.Prague: The Czech capital, whose Old Town astronomical clock dates from 1410 and still works. It has been the capital for centuries.
National capitals in Europe.Warsaw: Poland's capital was rebuilt almost entirely after World War II, and even its Old Town was reconstructed from paintings.
National capitals in Europe.Dublin: The Irish capital, where the Vikings founded a settlement. The name comes from the Irish for 'black pool'.
National capitals in Europe.Oslo: Norway's capital, founded around 1048, renamed Christiania for centuries before it went back to Oslo in 1925.
National capitals in Europe.Helsinki: Finland's capital, on the Baltic, founded in 1550 and made capital in 1812 by the Russian tsar. It's among the world's most northerly capitals.
National capitals in Europe.Barcelona: A trap: Spain's second city, but Madrid is the capital. It's famous for Gaudí's architecture.
National capitals in Europe.Milan: Italy's fashion and finance centre, but Rome is the capital. Its Gothic cathedral took about 600 years to complete.
National capitals in Europe.Munich: Bavaria's capital and a big city of Germany, but not the national capital, which is Berlin. It hosts Oktoberfest.
National capitals in Europe.Zurich: A trap: Switzerland's largest city and financial hub, but the Swiss capital is Bern, a much smaller city.
National capitals in Europe.Geneva: A trap: home to the UN's European headquarters and the Red Cross, but not the Swiss capital, which is Bern.
National capitals in Europe.Istanbul: The largest city in Turkey, once the capital of Byzantium and Ottoman empires, but Ankara has been Turkey's capital since 1923.
National capitals in Europe.Krakow: Poland's old royal capital until 1596 and still the cultural heart, but Warsaw is the capital.
National capitals in Europe.Porto: A trap: Portugal's second city and the home of port wine, but the national capital is Lisbon.
National capitals in Europe.Rotterdam: Home of Europe's busiest port, but Amsterdam is the Dutch capital, and The Hague hosts the government.
National capitals in Europe.Manchester: England's former industrial powerhouse, birthplace of the Industrial Revolution, but not capital.
National capitals in Europe.Venice: A trap: the famous city of canals is built on over 100 small islands, but Rome is Italy's capital.
National capitals in Europe.Lyon: France's gastronomic capital, thanks to chefs like Paul Bocuse. Third in size, and not capital.
National capitals in Europe.Hamburg: A trap: Germany's biggest port and second-largest city, but Berlin is the capital.

Places in Thailand.Bangkok: Its full ceremonial name is among the longest place names in the world, with over 160 letters, though Thais call it Krung Thep.
Places in Thailand.Chiang Mai: Founded in 1296, this northern city has over 300 temples, and each November it lights thousands of lanterns for the Yi Peng festival.
Places in Thailand.Krabi: Known for limestone cliffs, which attract rock climbers from all over the world, and for the beaches at Railay, reachable only by boat.
Places in Thailand.Ko Samui: Thailand's second-largest island is famed for coconuts, and it exports millions of them every year.
Places in Thailand.Ko Phi Phi: Maya Bay on Phi Phi Leh was the setting of the film The Beach, and it was closed for years to let the coral recover.
Places in Thailand.Pattaya: A beach city about two hours southeast of Bangkok, which grew from a fishing village into a resort after US troops arrived in the 1960s.
Places in Thailand.Ayutthaya: The capital of the Siamese kingdom for over 400 years until Burmese forces sacked it in 1767; its ruins are a UNESCO World Heritage site.
Places in Thailand.Ko Tao: The island's name means Turtle Island, and it is one of the world's busiest places to get scuba diving certificates.
Places in Thailand.Hua Hin: Thailand's oldest beach resort became fashionable after the royal family built a summer palace there in the 1920s.
Places in Thailand.Chiang Rai: Its White Temple, Wat Rong Khun, is a dazzling modern work by the artist Chalermchai Kositpipat, and it is still being built.
Places in Thailand.Wat Arun: The Temple of Dawn rises on the Chao Phraya River in Bangkok, and its central spire is decorated with colored porcelain.
Places in Thailand.Bali: An Indonesian island known as the Island of the Gods, and most of its people practice a unique form of Hindu religion.
Places in Thailand.Langkawi: A Malaysian archipelago of 99 islands, duty-free since 1987, and it lies just south of the Thai border.
Places in Thailand.Penang: A Malaysian island whose George Town is a UNESCO site renowned for street food and for wall murals.
Places in Thailand.Siem Reap: The Cambodian gateway to Angkor Wat, a vast temple complex built in the twelfth century, and it is not in Thailand.
Places in Thailand.Luang Prabang: A Laotian town of golden temples where monks collect alms at dawn, and it sits on the Mekong River.
Places in Thailand.Ha Long Bay: Vietnam's bay of nearly 2,000 limestone islands, whose name means descending dragon; it is not Thai.
Places in Thailand.Hoi An: A Vietnamese trading port famous for its lantern-lit old town and tailors, and it sits on the central coast.
Places in Thailand.Boracay: A Philippine island with a white sand beach about four kilometers long, popular with tourists.
Places in Thailand.Palawan: A Philippine island whose Puerto Princesa Underground River is one of the New 7 Wonders of Nature.
Places in Thailand.Phnom Penh: The capital of Cambodia sits where the Mekong and Tonle Sap rivers meet, far from Thailand.
Places in Thailand.Lombok: The Indonesian island east of Bali, dominated by the Rinjani volcano, with quieter beaches than its neighbor.
Places in Thailand.Yangon: The largest city in Myanmar, home to the gilded Shwedagon Pagoda, and Myanmar is a neighbor of Thailand, not part of it.

Places that are also a food or drink.Java: The Indonesian island lent its name to coffee, as the Dutch grew coffee there in the 1700s.
Places that are also a food or drink.Cayenne: The pepper takes its name from the capital of French Guiana, and the powder is a ground form of dried chilis.

Organs found in the abdomen.Liver: The largest internal organ, which can regrow after part of it is removed. It performs hundreds of tasks, from detoxifying blood to making bile.
Organs found in the abdomen.Stomach: Its acid is strong enough to dissolve metal, so the lining renews itself every few days to avoid digesting itself.
Organs found in the abdomen.Pancreas: A gland tucked behind the stomach that makes both digestive enzymes and insulin. Its name means all flesh in Greek.
Organs found in the abdomen.Spleen: It filters old red blood cells and stores immune cells. People can live without it, though infections become more dangerous.
Organs found in the abdomen.Gallbladder: A small pouch under the liver storing bile, a fat-digesting fluid. You can live fine without it, and removing it is a common surgery.
Organs found in the abdomen.Kidneys: These bean-shaped organs filter about 180 liters of blood each day, though only about a liter or two ends up as urine.
Organs found in the abdomen.Small intestine: It's about 6 meters long, much longer than the large intestine, and is where most nutrients are absorbed.
Organs found in the abdomen.Large intestine: It's shorter but wider than the small intestine, and absorbs water. Trillions of bacteria live there.
Organs found in the abdomen.Appendix: A small pouch off the large intestine. It may serve as a safe house for helpful gut bacteria, and removing it is routine surgery.
Organs found in the abdomen.Heart: A trap: it sits in the chest, not the abdomen. Beating about 100,000 times a day, it's protected by the ribcage.
Organs found in the abdomen.Lungs: A trap: they are in the chest, above the diaphragm. Stretched flat, their air sacs would cover a tennis court.
Organs found in the abdomen.Brain: A trap: it's in the head. It uses about a fifth of the body's energy despite being about 2 percent of its weight.
Organs found in the abdomen.Thyroid: A trap: this butterfly-shaped gland sits in the neck, not the abdomen, and its hormones set the body's metabolic pace.
Organs found in the abdomen.Thymus: A trap: it's in the upper chest, behind the sternum. It trains immune T cells, and shrinks after puberty.
Organs found in the abdomen.Larynx: A trap: the voice box sits in the neck, at the top of the windpipe, and the Adam's apple is part of it, not the abdomen.
Organs found in the abdomen.Trachea: A trap: the windpipe runs through the neck and chest. It's held open by C-shaped cartilage rings.
Organs found in the abdomen.Tonsils: A trap: these lymph-tissue lumps sit at the back of the throat, not the abdomen, and help catch germs entering the mouth.
Organs found in the abdomen.Eyes: A trap: they're in the head. Each is held in a bony socket and moved by six muscles.
Organs found in the abdomen.Tongue: A trap: it's in the mouth. It's a group of muscles, and its print is as unique as a fingerprint.
Organs found in the abdomen.Pituitary gland: A trap: a pea-sized gland at the base of the brain, nicknamed the master gland because it controls other hormone glands.
Organs found in the abdomen.Pineal gland: A trap: a tiny gland deep in the brain that makes melatonin. Descartes thought it was the seat of the soul.
Organs found in the abdomen.Vocal cords: A trap: they're in the larynx, in the neck. They vibrate hundreds of times a second to produce your voice.
Organs found in the abdomen.Sinuses: A trap: air-filled spaces in the skull around the nose and eyes. They lighten the head and add resonance to the voice.
Organs found in the abdomen.Eardrum: A trap: a thin membrane in the ear, about 8 to 10 millimeters across, that vibrates with sound.

Elements your body needs to survive.Carbon: Carbon makes up about 18 percent of your body weight. Its ability to bond in long chains is why life on Earth is carbon-based.
Elements your body needs to survive.Hydrogen: Most of the atoms in your body are hydrogen, mostly in water. Nearly all of that hydrogen dates from the Big Bang.
Elements your body needs to survive.Oxygen: It's about 65 percent of your body weight, mostly as water. Your cells use it to burn food for energy.
Elements your body needs to survive.Nitrogen: Part of every protein and all your DNA. Though air is 78 percent nitrogen, you can't use it from air and must get it from food.
Elements your body needs to survive.Calcium: About 99 percent of your calcium is stored in bones and teeth. The rest helps muscles contract and nerves fire.
Elements your body needs to survive.Phosphorus: Forms the backbone of DNA and the energy molecule ATP. It was first isolated in 1669 from boiled-down urine.
Elements your body needs to survive.Potassium: Essential for nerves and heart rhythm. Bananas are known for it, though potatoes and beans often have more.
Elements your body needs to survive.Sulfur: Found in several amino acids, and it gives eggs and garlic their smell. Hair is strengthened by sulfur bonds, which is also why burnt hair smells.
Elements your body needs to survive.Sodium: You need it for nerve signals and fluid balance. A pure form explodes in water, though in table salt it is harmless.
Elements your body needs to survive.Chlorine: A poisonous gas on its own, but the chloride in salt is vital. Your stomach uses it to make hydrochloric acid.
Elements your body needs to survive.Magnesium: Needed by hundreds of enzymes, and at the center of chlorophyll in plants. Nuts, seeds and leafy greens supply it.
Elements your body needs to survive.Iron: Sits at the heart of hemoglobin, carrying oxygen in your blood. That is why blood is red, and why iron lack causes anemia.
Elements your body needs to survive.Zinc: A trace element needed by hundreds of enzymes, and for immunity and wound healing. Oysters are very rich in it.
Elements your body needs to survive.Iodine: Needed by the thyroid for hormones. Adding it to table salt in the 1920s almost wiped out goiter in many regions.
Elements your body needs to survive.Gold: Not needed by the body. Though edible in tiny amounts and sometimes used in fancy food, it does nothing nutritionally.
Elements your body needs to survive.Uranium: No role in the body, and it's radioactive and chemically toxic to kidneys. Trace amounts exist in soil and food, though.
Elements your body needs to survive.Neon: A noble gas that doesn't react with anything, so your body can't use it. It is what makes bright signs glow red-orange.
Elements your body needs to survive.Helium: An inert gas, harmless but unused by your body. Breathing it makes your voice squeaky because sound travels faster through it.
Elements your body needs to survive.Argon: A noble gas that makes up nearly 1 percent of air. You breathe it all day, but it plays no part in your biology.
Elements your body needs to survive.Plutonium: A man-made, radioactive metal with no biological role. Only trace amounts exist in nature, and it is highly hazardous.
Elements your body needs to survive.Radon: A radioactive gas that seeps from the ground into basements. No use to the body, and a leading cause of lung cancer in non-smokers.
Elements your body needs to survive.Xenon: A heavy noble gas that does nothing in the body, though it can be used as an anesthetic and in car headlights.
Elements your body needs to survive.Krypton: A noble gas with no role in biology. Its name means 'hidden', and it was once used to define the meter.
Elements your body needs to survive.Platinum: A rare precious metal not needed by the body, though platinum-based drugs such as cisplatin are used against cancer.

Electronic dance music styles.House: House takes its name from Chicago's Warehouse club, where DJ Frankie Knuckles shaped the sound in the early 1980s.
Electronic dance music styles.Techno: Techno was shaped in Detroit in the mid-1980s by the Belleville Three: Juan Atkins, Derrick May and Kevin Saunderson.
Electronic dance music styles.Trance: Trance runs at about 130 to 140 beats per minute, built on long repeating melodies and slow, dramatic breakdowns.
Electronic dance music styles.Dubstep: Dubstep grew in South London around 2000, defined by sparse beats and sub-bass so deep you feel it in your chest.
Electronic dance music styles.Drum and bass: Drum and bass races at around 170 beats per minute, pairing frantic broken beats with deep, rolling basslines.
Electronic dance music styles.Jungle: Jungle came before drum and bass in early-1990s Britain, built on chopped breakbeats like the famous Amen break.
Electronic dance music styles.Hardstyle: Hardstyle came out of the Netherlands in the late 1990s, with a heavily distorted, pitch-bent kick drum as its signature.
Electronic dance music styles.Breakbeat: Breakbeat is built on sampled or looped drum breaks, often borrowed from old funk records, and it fathered jungle.
Electronic dance music styles.Eurodance: Eurodance ruled 1990s charts with acts like Snap! and 2 Unlimited, mixing rapped verses with sung choruses.
Electronic dance music styles.Big beat: Big beat, led by the Chemical Brothers and Fatboy Slim in the late 1990s, crashed rock energy into heavy breakbeats.
Electronic dance music styles.Bluegrass: Bluegrass is acoustic Appalachian music with banjo and fiddle, named for Bill Monroe's Blue Grass Boys.
Electronic dance music styles.Polka: Polka is a bouncy Central European dance in two-quarter time, born in 19th-century Bohemia, and it's not electronic.
Electronic dance music styles.Reggae: Reggae grew from Jamaican ska and rocksteady, driven by offbeat guitar chops and a heavy bass, far from club synths.
Electronic dance music styles.Bebop: Bebop is fast, complex jazz from the 1940s, played by small combos like Charlie Parker's, not made for dance floors.
Electronic dance music styles.Swing: Swing was the big-band dance music of the 1930s and '40s, and it relied on live horn sections, not synthesizers.
Electronic dance music styles.Grunge: Grunge is distorted guitar rock from Seattle, with Nirvana its best-known act, and a very different sound from club music.
Electronic dance music styles.Punk: Punk is fast, raw, short guitar music, a rock offshoot, with no place for the synths and drum machines of dance music.
Electronic dance music styles.Gospel: Gospel is church-born vocal music, rooted in choirs and call-and-response, far from the electronic dance floor.
Electronic dance music styles.Opera: Opera is sung theatre with a full orchestra, performed without amplification, so it's about as far from EDM as it gets.
Electronic dance music styles.Flamenco: Flamenco is Spanish guitar, singing and dance, performed live with handclaps, from Andalusia, not an electronic style.
Electronic dance music styles.Soul: Soul grew from gospel and R&B, with voices like Aretha Franklin's at the center, rather than programmed beats.
Electronic dance music styles.Country: Country is guitar-led storytelling music from the American South, centered in Nashville, rather than dance electronica.
Electronic dance music styles.Bossa nova: Bossa nova is a mellow Brazilian blend of samba and jazz, famous through The Girl from Ipanema, and not electronic.
Electronic dance music styles.Ska: Ska is a quick, offbeat-driven Jamaican style that came before reggae, played with live horns rather than synths.

Guitar brands.Fender: Leo Fender's Telecaster of 1950 is often called the first commercially successful solid-body electric guitar, and its basic design is still in production.
Guitar brands.Gibson: The Les Paul is named for the guitarist and inventor who helped design it, and Gibson's 1959 models are now worth well over a million dollars.
Guitar brands.Martin: Martin has built acoustics in Pennsylvania since 1833, and its dreadnought body shape became the standard for country and folk guitars.

Guitar brands.Rickenbacker: Its jangly twelve-string was played by George Harrison on A Hard Day's Night and by Roger McGuinn, shaping the sound of folk rock.
Guitar brands.PRS: Paul Reed Smith opened a small Maryland workshop in 1985, and Carlos Santana's loyalty helped turn it into a premium brand.
Guitar brands.Yamaha: Better known for pianos and motorcycles, this Japanese firm began as a reed organ maker in 1887 and now makes guitars too.
Guitar brands.Washburn: One of the oldest American guitar names, it dates to the 1880s and began in Chicago making guitars sold to mail-order customers.
Guitar brands.Squier: This is Fender's budget line, named for a string-making company Fender bought in 1965, and it is where many beginners start.
Guitar brands.Steinway: This is a piano maker, not a guitar brand: Steinway's concert grands, made in New York and Hamburg, are the standard on most major stages.
Guitar brands.Bösendorfer: Founded in Vienna in 1828, it makes pianos with extra bass keys, and some models reach a rare nine octaves of range.
Guitar brands.Stradivarius: Antonio Stradivari made violins in Cremona around 1700, and fewer than 600 instruments survive, some selling for millions of dollars.
Guitar brands.Selmer: Founded in France, Selmer is famous for saxophones, and its Mark VI is still a prized model among jazz players decades after production stopped.
Guitar brands.Zildjian: Cymbal makers since 1623 in Istanbul, the Zildjian family has kept its alloy formula a closely guarded secret for centuries.
Guitar brands.Ludwig: William Ludwig built the drums Ringo Starr played, and the Beatles' Ludwig kit with its drop-T logo is one of rock's most famous images.
Guitar brands.Moog: Robert Moog's synthesizers of the 1960s made electronic sound a pop sound, and his name still stands for the analog synth.
Guitar brands.Hammond: Laurens Hammond's electric organ of 1935 used spinning tone wheels instead of pipes, and it became essential to jazz, gospel and rock.
Guitar brands.Marshall: Marshall makes amplifiers, not guitars, and Jim Marshall's stacks, first made in 1962 in a London shop, defined loud rock for generations.
Guitar brands.Bose: This company makes audio equipment, not guitars, and was founded in 1964 by an MIT professor who studied how people actually hear.
Guitar brands.Sennheiser: This German firm, founded in 1945, makes microphones and headphones, not guitars, and its mics are staples in broadcast and studio.
Guitar brands.Shure: Shure's SM58 vocal microphone, introduced in 1966, is among the most used stage mics ever, and it is famously hard to break.

Playground games.Mahjong: A tile game from China, which is played at tables.
