Contract bridge terms.Trump: Any card of the suit that outranks all others in a hand. The word is just a corruption of triumph, centuries before it was anyone's surname.
Contract bridge terms.Dummy: Declarer's partner lays their cards face up and takes no part in the play. Dummy's cards are still played, just by someone else.
Contract bridge terms.Rubber: A match won by the first side to take two games, so a rubber lasts at most three. The word also appears in whist and, oddly, in cricket and bowls.
Contract bridge terms.Trick: One round of four cards, one from each player, won by the highest card. Bridge is really a game of taking tricks, and contracts are promises about how many.
Contract bridge terms.Bid: A promise to win a set number of tricks, usually with a named trump suit. The auction is where a pair's whole game plan is secretly negotiated.
Contract bridge terms.Slam: A contract to win 12 of 13 tricks is a small slam, and all 13 is a grand slam. The word later migrated to tennis and Grand Slam tournaments.
Contract bridge terms.Contract: The final bid that decides how many tricks declarer must take. The name of the game itself comes from this, and it is also called contract bridge.
Contract bridge terms.No trump: A hand played with no trump suit, so the highest card in the suit led always wins. It scores more per trick than a minor suit, which makes it popular.
Contract bridge terms.Declarer: The player who first named the suit of the final contract and plays both their own hand and the dummy. Everyone else defends against them.
Contract bridge terms.Vulnerable: A side that has won a game toward the rubber, so bonuses and penalties are bigger. Being vulnerable raises the stakes, which changes how boldly people bid.
Contract bridge terms.Finesse: A way to win a trick with a lower card by gambling that the opponent holding a higher one sits in the right seat. It's a coin flip dressed up as skill.
Contract bridge terms.Ruff: To play a trump on a trick when you have no cards in the suit led. The word comes from the old French game ronfle, and it works as a surprise weapon.
Contract bridge terms.Redouble: A bid that doubles the doubling of a contract, raising the stakes again. It's rare, and usually means someone is very sure they will make it.
Contract bridge terms.Checkmate: A chess term, not a bridge one. It comes from the Persian shah mat, often translated as the king is helpless.
Contract bridge terms.Gambit: A chess opening that sacrifices material for position. The word comes from the Italian for tripping someone up, a wrestling move.
Contract bridge terms.Rook: A chess piece that moves in straight lines. Oddly, the card game Rook doesn't use a rook, and in bridge the word only means to cheat.
Contract bridge terms.Bluff: Bridge allows psychic bids, but this is poker's main weapon. A bluff in bridge is risky because your partner can be misled as well as the opponents.
Contract bridge terms.Ante: A small forced bet placed in poker before cards are dealt. Bridge uses no money on the table, as the stakes are in the scoring.
Contract bridge terms.Flop: In Texas hold'em, the first three community cards dealt face up. Bridge has no community cards; every hand is private.
Contract bridge terms.River: The fifth and last community card in Texas hold'em. It's a poker term and has no place in bridge, where all 52 cards go to the players.
Contract bridge terms.Yahtzee: A dice game where five of a kind scores 50 points. It was popularized in 1956 by a couple who learned it on a yacht, hence the name.
Contract bridge terms.Gin: A two-player rummy card game, also a spirit. Gin rummy gets its name from the drink, and has nothing to do with bridge's partnerships.
Contract bridge terms.Meld: A set or run of cards laid down in rummy games. Bridge has no melds, though pinochle does, using the same word.
Contract bridge terms.Birdie: A golf term for one stroke under par. It comes from 1890s American slang, where bird meant something excellent.

Built by the ancient Romans.Colosseum: Opened in AD 80, it held perhaps 50,000 spectators and had a network of lifts and trapdoors under the arena floor to raise animals and scenery.
Built by the ancient Romans.Pantheon: Its unreinforced concrete dome, completed around AD 126, is still the world's largest of its kind. A round hole, the oculus, lights the whole interior.
Built by the ancient Romans.Hadrian's Wall: The Roman frontier across northern Britain, about 117 km long, begun around AD 122. Soldiers manned small forts every Roman mile along it.
Built by the ancient Romans.Pont du Gard: A three-tiered aqueduct bridge in southern France, nearly 50 m high. It carried water to Nîmes, dropping only about 2.5 cm per 100 m of the channel.
Built by the ancient Romans.Circus Maximus: Rome's great chariot-racing track, which could seat well over 150,000 people. Races ran for centuries on a stretch that is now a public park.
Built by the ancient Romans.Appian Way: The "queen of roads", begun in 312 BC to link Rome with southern Italy. After the slave revolt of Spartacus, 6,000 rebels were crucified along it.
Built by the ancient Romans.Arch of Titus: Built after AD 81 to mark the capture of Jerusalem. Its relief shows Roman soldiers carrying off the menorah from the Temple.
Built by the ancient Romans.Trajan's Column: A 30 m column in Rome whose spiral carving tells the story of Trajan's Dacian wars in about 2,500 figures. Unrolled, the band runs some 200 m.
Built by the ancient Romans.Baths of Caracalla: Public baths completed around AD 216, they could hold 1,600 bathers and included libraries and gardens. Today they host open-air operas.
Built by the ancient Romans.Arch of Constantine: Dedicated in AD 315 near the Colosseum, it recycled sculptures from earlier emperors' monuments, a salvage job that shows its age.
Built by the ancient Romans.Parthenon: Greek, not Roman. It was built in the 440s BC in Athens for the goddess Athena, centuries before Rome ruled Greece.
Built by the ancient Romans.Acropolis: Athens's rock-top citadel, a Greek site where the Parthenon stands. Rome added to it but did not build it.
Built by the ancient Romans.Great Wall of China: Built by successive Chinese dynasties, mostly in Ming times. Rome and China never really dealt with each other directly, but did swap silk.
Built by the ancient Romans.Stonehenge: A prehistoric monument in England, started around 3000 BC, long before Rome existed. The Romans arrived in Britain only in AD 43.
Built by the ancient Romans.Taj Mahal: A Mughal tomb in India, completed in the 1640s for Shah Jahan's wife Mumtaz Mahal. It lies about 1,500 years after Rome's peak.
Built by the ancient Romans.Machu Picchu: An Inca mountain estate in Peru from the 1400s, built with no mortar and no contact with Rome.
Built by the ancient Romans.Tower of Pisa: A medieval Italian bell tower whose lean began during construction in the 1170s because the soil was soft. Italian, but not Roman.
Built by the ancient Romans.Eiffel Tower: Built for the 1889 World's Fair in Paris by Gustave Eiffel's company. Wrought iron, and about 1,800 years too late.
Built by the ancient Romans.Angkor Wat: A 12th-century Khmer temple in Cambodia, the largest religious monument in the world. It was built in Asia, far beyond Roman reach.
Built by the ancient Romans.Petra: Carved into rose-coloured cliffs in Jordan by the Nabataeans. Rome annexed it in AD 106 but the monuments are Nabataean work.
Built by the ancient Romans.Alhambra: A Moorish palace-fortress in Granada, mostly from the 13th and 14th centuries. Islamic Spain built it long after Rome fell.
Built by the ancient Romans.Chichen Itza: A Maya city in Mexico with the El Castillo pyramid. At the equinox, a serpent-shaped shadow seems to slither down its steps.
Built by the ancient Romans.Trevi Fountain: It stands in Rome but is Baroque, completed in 1762. It is fed by an aqueduct the Romans did build, Aqua Virgo, which dates to 19 BC.
Built by the ancient Romans.Spanish Steps: A Roman landmark finished in 1725, so it is Baroque, not ancient. The name comes from the nearby Spanish embassy.

Soviet side of the Space Race.Sputnik: The first artificial satellite, launched by the USSR on 4 October 1957. Its beeping signal shocked the West and kicked off the Space Race.
Soviet side of the Space Race.Laika: A stray Moscow dog sent into orbit on Sputnik 2 in 1957. She was the first animal to orbit Earth but did not survive the flight.
Soviet side of the Space Race.Yuri Gagarin: In April 1961 he became the first human in space, circling Earth once in 108 minutes. He was 27.
Soviet side of the Space Race.Valentina Tereshkova: In 1963 she became the first woman in space, orbiting Earth 48 times aboard Vostok 6. She was a textile worker and parachutist.
Soviet side of the Space Race.Vostok 1: The craft that carried Gagarin in 1961. Its name means 'East', and he landed by ejecting and parachuting separately.
Soviet side of the Space Race.Alexei Leonov: In 1965 he made the first spacewalk, and his suit ballooned so much he had to bleed air just to get back inside.
Soviet side of the Space Race.Salyut 1: The first space station, launched in 1971. Its first crew died on return when a valve opened and the cabin lost air.
Soviet side of the Space Race.Luna 9: The Soviet probe that made the first soft landing on the Moon in 1966, sending back the first photographs from the surface.
Soviet side of the Space Race.Sergei Korolev: The chief designer behind Sputnik and Gagarin's flight. His identity was a state secret until after his death in 1966.
Soviet side of the Space Race.Apollo 11: Trap: this was America's triumph. In 1969 the Apollo 11 mission landed the first people on the Moon.
Soviet side of the Space Race.Neil Armstrong: Trap: first person on the Moon, in 1969. He's the American answer to Gagarin, not part of the Soviet side.
Soviet side of the Space Race.Buzz Aldrin: Trap: second person on the Moon. He's American, and he was the one who coined the phrase 'magnificent desolation'.
Soviet side of the Space Race.John Glenn: Trap: first American to orbit Earth, in 1962, about a year after Gagarin. NASA, not the USSR.
Soviet side of the Space Race.Alan Shepard: Trap: the first American in space, in 1961, but only on a short suborbital hop, weeks after Gagarin.
Soviet side of the Space Race.Explorer 1: Trap: America's first satellite, launched in 1958 after Sputnik. It discovered the Van Allen radiation belts.
Soviet side of the Space Race.Skylab: Trap: the first American space station, launched in 1973. It outlasted its missions and fell to Earth in 1979.
Soviet side of the Space Race.Space Shuttle: Trap: a reusable NASA spacecraft flying from 1981 to 2011. The Soviets built a lookalike, Buran, which flew once without crew.
Soviet side of the Space Race.Gemini: Trap: NASA's two-person program of the mid-1960s that rehearsed docking and spacewalks for the Moon.
Soviet side of the Space Race.Wernher von Braun: Trap: the German rocket engineer who built the V-2, then led NASA's Saturn V team after moving to America.
Soviet side of the Space Race.Sally Ride: Trap: first American woman in space, in 1983. She was also a physicist and later an author of children's science books.
Soviet side of the Space Race.Ham the chimp: Trap: a chimpanzee NASA launched in 1961 to test that a primate could work controls in space. He survived.
Soviet side of the Space Race.Hubble: Trap: an American telescope launched in 1990. Its first images were blurry because of a mirror flaw, fixed in 1993.
Soviet side of the Space Race.Saturn V: Trap: NASA's giant Moon rocket of the 1960s and 70s. The Soviet rival, the N1, failed on all four test launches.
Soviet side of the Space Race.Apollo 13: Trap: the 1970 NASA mission that nearly ended in disaster when an oxygen tank exploded. The crew survived.

Things you'd find under a couch cushion.Coins: Sofa cushions flex when you sit, opening a gap that swallows loose change, which is why shaking out the couch can pay off.
Things you'd find under a couch cushion.Crumbs: Dust mites in sofas feed mostly on shed human skin flakes; crumbs mainly attract ants and other opportunists.
Things you'd find under a couch cushion.TV remote: Zenith's 1955 Flash-Matic, the first wireless TV remote, used a beam of light, and sunlight could accidentally change channels.
Things you'd find under a couch cushion.Popcorn: Popcorn kernels pop when trapped water turns to steam at about 180 C, bursting the hull and turning the starch inside out.
Things you'd find under a couch cushion.Hair tie: Rommy Revson patented the scrunchie in 1987; the soft fabric-covered band was meant to be gentler on hair.
Things you'd find under a couch cushion.Pen: The ballpoint pen was patented in 1938 by Hungarian journalist László Bíró, who noticed newspaper ink dried fast.
Things you'd find under a couch cushion.Bobby pin: Its flat, springy shape slips easily into narrow gaps, which is exactly why it vanishes into upholstery seams.
Things you'd find under a couch cushion.Guitar pick: Players buy picks by the bag because they vanish constantly; the classic teardrop shape is known as the 351.
Things you'd find under a couch cushion.Lego brick: Bricks made today still click with ones from 1958, built to tolerances of a tiny fraction of a millimeter.
Things you'd find under a couch cushion.Phone charger: Modern fast chargers can push many times the power of the early 5-watt phone chargers that fall behind cushions.
Things you'd find under a couch cushion.Receipt: Many thermal receipts are printed without ink, using heat-sensitive paper, which is why they fade in sun or heat.
Things you'd find under a couch cushion.Earring: Pierced ears are seen on Ötzi the Iceman, who lived about 5,300 years ago, so ear jewelry has long been losing itself.
Things you'd find under a couch cushion.Bottle cap: A standard crown cap has 21 teeth, a design William Painter patented in 1892.
Things you'd find under a couch cushion.Refrigerator: Far too large to hide; couches do hoard surprising things, but a fridge weighs well over 80 kilograms.
Things you'd find under a couch cushion.Bathtub: Absurdly big; ancient Cretan palaces had clay bathtubs by around 1700 BCE, but none were hiding in the furniture.
Things you'd find under a couch cushion.Grand piano: Concert grands weigh over 450 kilograms, so the only thing hiding under that cushion is a stray guitar pick.
Things you'd find under a couch cushion.Ladder: Too long to hide; a Mesolithic cave painting in Spain shows honey gatherers on a rope ladder thousands of years ago.
Things you'd find under a couch cushion.Bicycle: Karl von Drais's 1817 'running machine' had no pedals; either way, it won't fit under a cushion.
Things you'd find under a couch cushion.Lawnmower: Edwin Budding patented the lawnmower in 1830, reportedly modeling it on a machine that trimmed cloth.
Things you'd find under a couch cushion.Washing machine: Too big; Alva Fisher's Thor machine of 1908 is often cited as the first electric washer.
Things you'd find under a couch cushion.Wardrobe: Only fiction's Narnia has a wardrobe that hides an entire world, in C. S. Lewis's 1950 novel.
Things you'd find under a couch cushion.Christmas tree: Too tall for a cushion gap; the decorated indoor tree tradition spread from 16th-century Germany.
Things you'd find under a couch cushion.Canoe: The oldest known canoe, from Pesse in the Netherlands, is roughly 10,000 years old.
Things you'd find under a couch cushion.Trampoline: George Nissen named it after the Spanish trampolín, a diving board, after building the first ones in the 1930s.

Things usually made of plastic.Lego brick: Lego bricks are made of ABS plastic, tolerances are tiny, and bricks from the 1950s still fit today's.
Things usually made of plastic.Water bottle: Disposable bottles are PET plastic, which can be recycled into polyester fibers for clothing.
Things usually made of plastic.Credit card: Cards are usually PVC plastic, and the standard size is set by an international standard, ID-1.
Things usually made of plastic.Toothbrush: Natural-bristle brushes gave way to nylon in 1938, and toothbrush handles are mostly plastic now.
Things usually made of plastic.Straw: Marvin Stone made the first paper straws in 1888 from rye grass, and plastic ones later took over.
Things usually made of plastic.Food container: Many tubs have a recycling number on the bottom, which shows the type of plastic, such as 5 for polypropylene.
Things usually made of plastic.Bucket: Most buckets are polyethylene, and the same plastic family is used for milk jugs.
Things usually made of plastic.Sippy cup: The spouted learner cup was designed to help toddlers move from bottle to cup with fewer spills.
Things usually made of plastic.Laundry basket: Many are made of polypropylene, a lightweight plastic that bends without breaking.
Things usually made of plastic.Shower curtain: The classic vinyl curtain's 'new shower curtain smell' comes from chemicals that evaporate from the plastic.
Things usually made of plastic.Sandwich bag: Resealable bags use a zip made of interlocking plastic tracks, an idea patented in 1950s.
Things usually made of plastic.Comb: Combs have been made from bone, wood, and ivory for thousands of years, and plastic ones began in the 1800s.
Things usually made of plastic.Bubble wrap: It began life in 1957 as a failed wallpaper, and its air-filled bubbles proved perfect for cushioning.
Things usually made of plastic.Wine glass: Wine glasses are made of glass or crystal, and plastic versions are mainly used outdoors and at parties.
Things usually made of plastic.Brick: Bricks are fired clay, which has been used for building for at least 5,000 years.
Things usually made of plastic.Coin: Coins are metal, and they use alloys like copper-nickel for durability.
Things usually made of plastic.Teapot: A teapot is usually ceramic, because it holds heat and doesn't affect the tea's flavor.
Things usually made of plastic.Wooden spoon: Wooden spoons don't scratch pans and don't conduct heat, so they stay cool in a hot pot.
Things usually made of plastic.Candle: Candles are usually paraffin, beeswax, or soy wax, and paraffin is itself a petroleum product.
Things usually made of plastic.Newspaper: Newsprint is cheap paper made from wood pulp, and it yellows because of lignin.
Things usually made of plastic.Wool scarf: Wool is a natural animal fiber, and its warmth comes from air trapped in its crimped structure.
Things usually made of plastic.Clay pot: Terracotta is fired clay, porous enough to let moisture pass, which keeps plants' roots from getting soggy.
Things usually made of plastic.Cast iron pan: Cast iron holds heat very evenly, and a well-seasoned pan can last for generations.
Things usually made of plastic.Pencil: A pencil is mostly wood and graphite, though some are made of plastic composite instead.

Things you'd pack in a toiletry bag.Toothbrush: Bristle toothbrushes date to China around 1498, where boar hair was attached to handles of bone or bamboo.
Things you'd pack in a toiletry bag.Toothpaste: Fluoride toothpaste became common in the mid-1900s, and it has helped cut cavities dramatically in the countries that use it.
Things you'd pack in a toiletry bag.Deodorant: Deodorant doesn't stop sweat; it blocks odor by killing or hiding the bacteria, while antiperspirants block sweat glands.
Things you'd pack in a toiletry bag.Razor: Safety razors were popularized by King Camp Gillette in the early 1900s, with disposable blades as the real innovation.
Things you'd pack in a toiletry bag.Shampoo: Shampoo comes from the Hindi word 'champo', meaning to press or massage, and arrived in Britain from India.
Things you'd pack in a toiletry bag.Comb: Combs are among the oldest tools humans have made, and examples of about 5,000 years old have been found in Egypt.
Things you'd pack in a toiletry bag.Dental floss: Flossing was first suggested by a New Orleans dentist in 1819, using silk thread.
Things you'd pack in a toiletry bag.Moisturizer: Moisturizer works by trapping water in the skin's top layer, so it's best applied right after washing.
Things you'd pack in a toiletry bag.Tweezers: Tweezers have been found in ancient tombs, and they were used for grooming in Egypt, Mesopotamia and the Indus Valley.
Things you'd pack in a toiletry bag.Nail clippers: Fingernails grow around 3 millimeters a month, and toenails grow roughly three times slower.
Things you'd pack in a toiletry bag.Lip balm: Lip balm was invented in the 1880s by a pharmacist named Charles Fleet, who sold it in little tubes.
Things you'd pack in a toiletry bag.Contact lens case: A contact lens case needs fresh solution every day, because storing lenses in old liquid breeds bacteria.
Things you'd pack in a toiletry bag.Laptop: A laptop is far too bulky for the toiletry bag and wants its own padded sleeve in your carry-on.
Things you'd pack in a toiletry bag.Passport: A passport is a document that belongs in your hand luggage, not in with the shampoo.
Things you'd pack in a toiletry bag.Phone charger: A phone charger is a tech item, so it goes with your electronics rather than with soap.
Things you'd pack in a toiletry bag.Paperback: A paperback is for the flight, not the bathroom bag, and it would not like water.
Things you'd pack in a toiletry bag.Swimsuit: A swimsuit goes with your clothes, but you'd pack a wet one in a separate bag.
Things you'd pack in a toiletry bag.Pajamas: Pajamas are clothing, so they go in the main bag instead of with toiletries.
Things you'd pack in a toiletry bag.Socks: Socks are clothing, and a handy tip is to tuck small items inside them to save space.
Things you'd pack in a toiletry bag.Flip-flops: Flip-flops go with shoes, and many travelers pack them for hostel showers.
Things you'd pack in a toiletry bag.Camera: A camera is valuable gear that needs padding and is better in your carry-on.
Things you'd pack in a toiletry bag.Headphones: Headphones are electronics, so they don't join the liquid items in the toiletry bag.
Things you'd pack in a toiletry bag.Travel pillow: A travel pillow is bulky comfort gear that clips to your luggage instead of fitting in a toiletry bag.
Things you'd pack in a toiletry bag.Snacks: Snacks are for the road; food in a toiletry bag could leak or attract ants.

Body parts that are also verbs.Elbow: You can elbow someone aside. The verb was in use in the 1600s, and it often means to push through a crowd.
Body parts that are also verbs.Shoulder: To shoulder a burden means to bear it. The verb also means to carry something on your shoulder.
Body parts that are also verbs.Hand: You can hand something over. The verb has been in use since the 1500s.
Body parts that are also verbs.Foot: To foot a bill means to pay it. The phrase came from totaling the amount at the bottom, or foot, of an account.
Body parts that are also verbs.Head: To head something means to lead it, as when you head a committee, and in soccer, to strike the ball with your head.
Body parts that are also verbs.Toe: To toe the line means to follow the rules. It might come from runners lining up their toes on a mark.
Body parts that are also verbs.Knee: To knee someone means to hit them with a knee. The verb is common in sports and fights.
Body parts that are also verbs.Eye: To eye something means to look at it carefully, and the verb is often used for sizing up a bargain.
Body parts that are also verbs.Nose: To nose around means to snoop. A nose also leads: boats nose into harbor.
Body parts that are also verbs.Mouth: To mouth words means to form them silently with your lips, like a lip reader.
Body parts that are also verbs.Stomach: To stomach something means to tolerate it, and it's often used for things hard to bear.
Body parts that are also verbs.Palm: To palm something means to hide it in your hand. Magicians do it to disappear coins.
Body parts that are also verbs.Thumb: To thumb a ride means to hitchhike, and thumbing through a book is to flip the pages.
Body parts that are also verbs.Liver: A liver is only a noun in everyday English, since to liver isn't a verb, though a liver is also someone who lives.
Body parts that are also verbs.Pancreas: The pancreas has no verb form in English. It's a noun only.
Body parts that are also verbs.Kidney: Kidney is a noun, though to kid is a different word that has nothing to do with it.
Body parts that are also verbs.Spleen: Spleen is a noun, though venting your spleen means giving vent to anger. It isn't a verb alone.
Body parts that are also verbs.Femur: Femur is only a noun, since the thigh bone has no verb use.
Body parts that are also verbs.Eyebrow: Eyebrow works as a noun in everyday speech, but 'to eyebrow' isn't standard. Raise an eyebrow, yes, but not eyebrow a thing.
Body parts that are also verbs.Navel: Navel is a noun with no everyday verb use, though navel-gazing is a phrase.
Body parts that are also verbs.Ankle: Ankle is a noun, though you may hear it used jokingly as a verb, as in to ankle out.
Body parts that are also verbs.Wrist: Wrist is a noun only. Wristing isn't standard English.
Body parts that are also verbs.Thigh: Thigh is a noun, though it has no common verb form.
Body parts that are also verbs.Hip: Hip is a noun, and also an adjective meaning trendy. It's not typically used as a verb.

Things too noisy for a library.Drum kit: A drum kit can reach over 100 decibels, which is why practice rooms are often soundproofed, and certainly why a library says no.
Things too noisy for a library.Trumpet: A trumpet can be heard from far away and tops 110 decibels, loud enough to disturb everyone in a quiet reading room.
Things too noisy for a library.Megaphone: A megaphone can project a voice for hundreds of meters, and in a library it would be heard everywhere.
Things too noisy for a library.Air horn: Air horns are made for boats and sports crowds and can top 120 decibels, so a library is the last place for one.
Things too noisy for a library.Bagpipes: Bagpipes are among the loudest acoustic instruments, around 110 decibels, which is louder than a chainsaw.
Things too noisy for a library.Leaf blower: A leaf blower can reach about 90 decibels at the operator's ear, loud enough to damage hearing over time.
Things too noisy for a library.Rooster: A rooster's crow can reach about 100 decibels, and roosters famously crow well before dawn.
Things too noisy for a library.Firecrackers: Firecrackers were invented in ancient China, where they were thought to scare away evil spirits with their bang.
Things too noisy for a library.Jackhammer: A jackhammer hits around 100 decibels or more, so even one working outside a library would shatter its quiet.
Things too noisy for a library.Karaoke machine: Karaoke is a Japanese word meaning empty orchestra, and it is a sound system that would be a disaster among the shelves.
Things too noisy for a library.Marching band: A marching band packs drums, brass, and cymbals into a booming, parade-style sound that would drown out any reader.
Things too noisy for a library.Library card: A library card is the key to a free borrowing system, and Benjamin Franklin helped found one of America's first lending libraries in 1731.
Things too noisy for a library.Book: Reading books silently is a surprisingly recent habit; in ancient times people usually read aloud, and Saint Augustine was amazed to see Ambrose read silently.
Things too noisy for a library.Reading glasses: Reading glasses are quiet, and Benjamin Franklin invented bifocals around 1784 for reading and distance.
Things too noisy for a library.Bookmark: A bookmark is a silent page-holder, and the oldest ones were simple ribbons or strips of leather tucked into a medieval manuscript.
Things too noisy for a library.Notebook: A notebook is almost silent, making only a quiet page rustle, which is why it is a library regular.
Things too noisy for a library.Pencil: A pencil scratches softly, and its core is graphite, a form of carbon, not lead, despite the common name lead.
Things too noisy for a library.Laptop: A laptop is quiet to use, aside from a clacky keyboard, and most libraries welcome one for study.
Things too noisy for a library.Tote bag: A tote bag is the book borrower's favorite, quiet and roomy enough for an armful of loans.
Things too noisy for a library.Headphones: Headphones keep sound from leaking out into the room, which is why libraries are full of people wearing them.
Things too noisy for a library.Backpack: A backpack is silent apart from a zipper, and it is the usual way students bring books and laptops to the library.
Things too noisy for a library.Sweater: A sweater is quiet and cozy, and libraries often keep the air cool to protect old books, so it is a handy layer.
Things too noisy for a library.Pen: A pen scratches quietly on paper, and the ballpoint was patented in 1888 by John J. Loud, a name that is ironic here.
Things too noisy for a library.Index cards: Index cards were the original library catalog system, and Swedish botanist Linnaeus pioneered their use in the 1700s.

Things heavier than an elephant.Blue whale: A blue whale weighs up to around 150 tonnes, roughly 25 elephants, and its heart alone is about the size of a small car.
Things heavier than an elephant.School bus: A school bus weighs about 10 tonnes or more, which is more than an African elephant at 4 to 6 tonnes.
Things heavier than an elephant.Locomotive: A diesel locomotive weighs well over 100 tonnes, around twenty elephants, to get traction to pull a very long train.
Things heavier than an elephant.Cruise ship: A big cruise ship displaces over 100,000 tonnes of water, as much as roughly 20,000 elephants.
Things heavier than an elephant.Jumbo jet: A fully loaded jumbo jet can weigh over 400 tonnes at takeoff, which is dozens of elephants in the air.
Things heavier than an elephant.Army tank: A main battle tank weighs around 60 tonnes, about ten elephants rolling along on metal tracks.
Things heavier than an elephant.Space shuttle: A space shuttle orbiter weighed about 80 tonnes empty, and with its tank and boosters, the launch stack weighed over 2,000 tonnes.
Things heavier than an elephant.Statue of Liberty: The Statue of Liberty weighs about 225 tonnes, roughly forty elephants, with a copper skin only about two pennies thick.
Things heavier than an elephant.Fire truck: A big fire engine can weigh 15 tonnes or more once loaded with water, well over an elephant.
Things heavier than an elephant.Whale shark: A whale shark, the largest fish, can top 15 tonnes, heavier than an elephant, yet it feeds mainly on plankton.
Things heavier than an elephant.Brachiosaurus: Brachiosaurus may have weighed 30 to 50 tonnes, up to ten elephants, and its neck helped it browse treetops.
Things heavier than an elephant.Cow: A cow weighs about 600 kilograms, far lighter than an elephant, though it still munches roughly 40 kilograms of feed a day.
Things heavier than an elephant.Horse: A horse weighs around 500 kilograms, a tenth of a big elephant, but it can sleep standing up.
Things heavier than an elephant.Car: A car weighs about 1.5 tonnes, which is lighter than an elephant, so it is a trap among heavy objects.
Things heavier than an elephant.Giraffe: A giraffe is the tallest animal but weighs only about 1,000 to 1,500 kilograms, less than an elephant.
Things heavier than an elephant.Piano: A concert grand piano weighs nearly 500 kilograms, which is heavy for movers but far lighter than an elephant.
Things heavier than an elephant.Gorilla: A big male gorilla weighs about 160 kilograms, and an elephant is roughly 30 times heavier.
Things heavier than an elephant.Polar bear: A big polar bear weighs up to around 700 kilograms, the largest land carnivore, but an elephant outweighs it several times.
Things heavier than an elephant.Motorcycle: A motorcycle weighs a couple of hundred kilograms, so even a big one is only a small fraction of an elephant.
Things heavier than an elephant.Moose: A moose is the largest deer, up to about 700 kilograms, and still nowhere near the weight of an elephant.
Things heavier than an elephant.Bison: An American bison can weigh up to a tonne, the heaviest land animal in North America, but far below an elephant.
Things heavier than an elephant.Kangaroo: A big red kangaroo weighs around 90 kilograms at most, and it hops at over 50 kilometers per hour.
Things heavier than an elephant.Lion: A male lion weighs about 190 kilograms, and an African elephant is some twenty or more times heavier.
Things heavier than an elephant.Camel: A camel weighs about 500 to 700 kilograms, with a hump that stores fat and not water, but it is no elephant.

Things in a car mechanic's garage.Car lift: Raises a vehicle so mechanics can work underneath. Two-post lifts can raise a car overhead in seconds.
Things in a car mechanic's garage.Socket set: Ratcheting sockets fit different bolt sizes. The ratchet lets mechanics turn bolts without lifting the tool off.
Things in a car mechanic's garage.Oil filter: Traps grit and metal flakes from engine oil. It's replaced at oil changes because it eventually clogs.
Things in a car mechanic's garage.Car jack: A jack lifts one corner of a vehicle. Mechanics always add jack stands since jacks alone can slip.
Things in a car mechanic's garage.Torque wrench: It clicks when a bolt reaches the right tightness. Wheel nuts need exact torque to avoid damage.
Things in a car mechanic's garage.Tire iron: A tool for removing lug nuts. The long handle gives extra leverage on tight nuts.
Things in a car mechanic's garage.Spark plugs: Each fires thousands of times a minute to ignite fuel in a gasoline engine. They're replaced periodically.
Things in a car mechanic's garage.Creeper: A low wheeled board that lets mechanics slide beneath cars. Its small wheels are designed to roll smoothly.
Things in a car mechanic's garage.Air compressor: Powers impact wrenches and inflates tires. Many garages store compressed air in a big tank.
Things in a car mechanic's garage.Engine hoist: A crane that lifts engines out of cars. A typical engine can weigh several hundred pounds.
Things in a car mechanic's garage.Jumper cables: Used to start dead batteries. Connecting them in the wrong order can cause sparks, so the order matters.
Things in a car mechanic's garage.Oil drain pan: Catches used oil during changes. Used motor oil can be recycled, so it shouldn't go in the trash.
Things in a car mechanic's garage.Dental chair: Reclines patients for dentists. It belongs in a dental clinic, not a garage.
Things in a car mechanic's garage.Pizza oven: Cooks pizzas at very high heat. A brick oven can reach about 800 degrees Fahrenheit, fit for a pizzeria.
Things in a car mechanic's garage.Pulpit: A raised platform in a church where sermons are delivered. Not found in garages.
Things in a car mechanic's garage.Hospital bed: Adjustable beds for patients. They belong in wards.
Things in a car mechanic's garage.Chalkboard: Used in classrooms and cafes. Mechanics usually use whiteboards or digital screens.
Things in a car mechanic's garage.Easel: Holds a painter's canvas upright. That's a studio item.
Things in a car mechanic's garage.Loom: A frame that weaves threads into cloth. Weavers use looms, not mechanics.
Things in a car mechanic's garage.Pottery wheel: Spins clay as a potter shapes it. A pottery studio item.
Things in a car mechanic's garage.Saddle: Rests on a horse. A bicycle saddle might lurk in a garage, but not this kind.
Things in a car mechanic's garage.Espresso machine: Forces hot water through coffee grounds under pressure. It belongs in a cafe.
Things in a car mechanic's garage.Treadmill: Gym equipment for running indoors. Not a mechanic's tool.
Things in a car mechanic's garage.Barber's chair: Reclining chair for haircuts. A barbershop item, not a garage one.

People who work in a school.Teacher: Teachers make thousands of small decisions every day, and research on teacher quality suggests it's among the biggest school factors in student success.
People who work in a school.Principal: The principal's name came from principal teacher, and the spelling differs from principle, which comes from a different word.
People who work in a school.Janitor: Janitor comes from Latin ianitor, a doorkeeper, named after Janus, the Roman god of doors and beginnings.
People who work in a school.Librarian: A school librarian does more than shelve books: they teach students how to find and judge reliable information.
People who work in a school.Counselor: School counselors help with grades, college plans and personal problems, and the typical U.S. school has far more students than the recommended per counselor.
People who work in a school.Cafeteria worker: Cafeteria staff may prepare hundreds of meals within a short lunch period, and the U.S. school lunch program began in 1946.
People who work in a school.School nurse: School nurses handle injuries, medication and illness, and one may serve several schools.
People who work in a school.Teaching assistant: Teaching assistants support students, especially those who need extra help, and in the UK TAs are a big part of classrooms.
People who work in a school.Coach: School coaches teach teamwork as well as sport, and many are also classroom teachers on top of coaching.
People who work in a school.Crossing guard: Crossing guards stop traffic so kids can walk safely, and many are volunteers or retirees with a stop sign paddle.
People who work in a school.Receptionist: The school receptionist is often the first person visitors meet, and the front desk is a school's nerve center.
People who work in a school.Bellhop: A bellhop carries bags in a hotel, and the name comes from the bell used to summon them.
People who work in a school.Sommelier: A sommelier is a restaurant's wine expert, and the French word originally meant a pack-animal driver.
People who work in a school.Croupier: A croupier runs casino tables, and the word comes from French for the rider behind on a horse's rump.
People who work in a school.Jockey: A jockey rides racehorses, and the word is a diminutive of Jock, a Scottish nickname.
People who work in a school.Bailiff: A bailiff keeps order in a courtroom, and in England they were once the king's agents who managed estates.
People who work in a school.Lumberjack: Lumberjacks fell trees, and the name comes from lumber, the old word for timber, plus jack, a man.
People who work in a school.Shepherd: Shepherd means sheep herder, and sheepdogs follow the shepherd's whistles and commands to move flocks.
People who work in a school.Flight attendant: Flight attendants are trained mainly for safety, and the first one in 1930 was Ellen Church.
People who work in a school.Lighthouse keeper: Lighthouse keepers tended the lamp and logged the weather, and automation has made the job nearly extinct.
People who work in a school.Ship's captain: A ship's captain is the ultimate authority aboard, and tradition says the captain should be the last to leave a sinking vessel.
People who work in a school.Farrier: A farrier shoes horses, and the word comes from Latin ferrum, iron.
People who work in a school.Midwife: Midwife means with woman in old English, and midwives help with births instead of working in a school.
People who work in a school.Stockbroker: Stockbrokers buy and sell shares for clients, and the New York Stock Exchange started under a buttonwood tree in 1792.

Things a barista uses.Espresso machine: Angelo Moriondo patented an early steam-powered espresso machine in Turin in 1884.
Things a barista uses.Steam wand: The steam wand heats and froths milk by injecting steam, and the fine microfoam it makes is what lets latte art pour.
Things a barista uses.Tamper: A tamper presses ground coffee evenly and firmly into the basket, since an uneven puck lets water rush through weak spots.
Things a barista uses.Portafilter: The portafilter holds the coffee grounds and locks into the machine, and its name mashes together 'portable' and 'filter'.
Things a barista uses.Coffee grinder: Freshly ground coffee loses aroma within minutes, which is why good cafes grind for each shot.
Things a barista uses.Milk jug: Baristas pour milk from a stainless-steel jug with a spout, and its shape matters when drawing latte art.
Things a barista uses.Knock box: A knock box is a bin where baristas bang out used coffee pucks, and that thump is a familiar cafe sound.
Things a barista uses.Coffee beans: Coffee beans are the seeds of a cherry-like fruit, and arabica and robusta are the two main species.
Things a barista uses.Paper cups: Paper cups usually carry a thin plastic lining, which makes many of them hard to recycle.
Things a barista uses.Coffee scale: Precision scales help baristas weigh both dose and shot to the gram for a consistent espresso.
Things a barista uses.Cocktail shaker: A cocktail shaker chills drinks with ice, and it's a bartender's tool, not a barista's.
Things a barista uses.Jigger: A jigger measures spirits, usually in one- and two-ounce sides, while baristas measure coffee on a scale.
Things a barista uses.Beer tap: Nitro cold brew is poured from a beer-style tap, so this one is a barista's cousin, though the classic beer tap is for pubs.
Things a barista uses.Wine decanter: A decanter lets wine breathe, and has nothing to do with the coffee bar.
Things a barista uses.Pizza peel: A pizza peel is a flat paddle for sliding pizzas in and out of ovens, which is a baker's tool.
Things a barista uses.Wok: A wok is a deep Chinese pan used for stir-frying at high heat, far from the coffee bar.
Things a barista uses.Fishing rod: A fishing rod is for anglers, though people do say a good brew can get you hooked.
Things a barista uses.Stethoscope: Doctors use stethoscopes, invented by René Laennec in 1816 using a rolled tube of paper.
Things a barista uses.Trowel: A trowel is a small hand shovel used by gardeners and bricklayers, not by a coffee bar.
Things a barista uses.Rolling pin: Bakers use rolling pins to flatten dough, and the tool dates back centuries.
Things a barista uses.Ice pick: An ice pick breaks big blocks of ice, which is a bar tool, whereas baristas just scoop cubes.
Things a barista uses.Meat cleaver: A cleaver's heavy blade chops through bone, so it's a butcher's tool, not a barista's.
Things a barista uses.Corkscrew: A corkscrew opens wine bottles, and modern designs go back to the 1600s.
Things a barista uses.Bottle opener: A bottle opener pops beer caps, and it's usually a bartender's gadget, as barista bottles are rare.

Accounting terms.Assets: Anything of value that a company owns, from cash and stock to buildings; the balance sheet shows they equal liabilities plus equity.
Accounting terms.Liabilities: Debts and obligations a company owes, such as loans and unpaid bills, and they sit opposite assets on the balance sheet.
Accounting terms.Equity: It is what remains for the owners after debts are subtracted, which is why it is sometimes called net worth.
Accounting terms.Revenue: It is the money a company earns from sales, called the top line because it sits at the very top of an income statement.
Accounting terms.Expenses: These are the costs of running a business, and subtracting them from revenue gives the profit, the so-called bottom line.
Accounting terms.Depreciation: It spreads the cost of an item such as a truck over its useful life, so the expense matches the years it earns money.
Accounting terms.Ledger: The ledger is the master record of all accounts, and double-entry bookkeeping in them dates back to medieval Italian merchants.
Accounting terms.Balance sheet: It is a snapshot of what a company owns and owes on one day, and the two sides must always balance, as the name says.
Accounting terms.Audit: An independent examiner checks the books for accuracy; the word comes from the Latin for "to hear", since early auditors listened to accounts read aloud.
Accounting terms.Accrual: Accrual accounting records income and costs when they are earned or incurred, not when cash actually changes hands.
Accounting terms.Debit: In double-entry bookkeeping every debit needs a matching credit; the word comes from the Latin "debere", to owe.
Accounting terms.Credit: Credit comes from the Latin "credere", to believe, and in accounting it records value flowing out of an account, so the books balance.
Accounting terms.Crescendo: A trap from music: it means gradually getting louder, and from the Italian for growing, but it has nothing to do with the books.
Accounting terms.Tempo: Italian for time, it sets the speed of a piece, and it is not a term for accounting.
Accounting terms.Chord: A chord is three or more notes sounded together, but a ledger has no use for harmony.
Accounting terms.Octave: It spans eight notes of a scale, and the frequency of a note doubles each octave, a music fact that accountants can skip.
Accounting terms.Staccato: It means notes played short and detached, from the Italian for detached, and it does not appear in a balance sheet.
Accounting terms.Treble clef: It is also called the G clef because its swirl circles the line where the note G sits, a music symbol with no accounting meaning.
Accounting terms.Harmony: Harmony is notes combining for pleasing effect; accountants would call it reconciliation when two sets of books agree.
Accounting terms.Allegro: It tells musicians to play fast and lively, and gives its name to whole movements of symphonies, but not to accounts.
Accounting terms.Sonata: It is a piece for one or two instruments, and the form shaped much of classical music, such as Beethoven's Moonlight Sonata.
Accounting terms.Arpeggio: Playing a chord's notes one after another, like a harp; the word comes from the Italian for harp-like.
Accounting terms.Fermata: This musical sign holds a note or rest for longer than written, so the performer decides how long, unlike the strict numbers in accounting.
Accounting terms.Glissando: A slide between notes, from the French for sliding, which is easy on trombone or violin but impossible on most keys of a piano.

Types of warship.Destroyer: Destroyers were created in the 1890s to destroy the new torpedo boats, and today they are among the most heavily armed surface ships.
Types of warship.Frigate: Once a fast sailing warship, the frigate is now a medium escort vessel focusing on submarine and air defense.
Types of warship.Corvette: A corvette is a small, fast warship, smaller than a frigate, used for coastal patrol and escort in many navies.
Types of warship.Cruiser: Cruisers once scouted far from the fleet; the name came from their long cruising range.
Types of warship.Submarine: The first military submarine, the Turtle, was a one-man wooden pod used in the American Revolution in 1776.
Types of warship.Aircraft carrier: A US supercarrier is a floating airbase with around 5,000 crew and displaces over 90,000 tons.
Types of warship.Minesweeper: They are often built of wood or fiberglass, so that they don't set off magnetic mines while clearing them.
Types of warship.Battleship: Battleships ruled until World War II, when aircraft carriers showed that air power could sink them from far away.
Types of warship.Patrol boat: Small, fast and lightly armed, patrol boats guard coasts and rivers, and are the workhorses of coast guards.
Types of warship.Dreadnought: HMS Dreadnought of 1906 was so advanced it made earlier battleships obsolete, and the name became a whole type.
Types of warship.Yacht: A yacht is a pleasure vessel, from Dutch "jacht" meaning hunt, and some superyachts exceed 100 meters.
Types of warship.Canoe: Canoes are some of the oldest boats; the oldest known one, the Pesse canoe, is around 10,000 years old.
Types of warship.Gondola: Gondolas are asymmetrical, built slightly lopsided so the single oarsman can steer in a straight line.
Types of warship.Kayak: Inuit hunters built kayaks from sealskin over a frame, and the word means hunter's boat.
Types of warship.Pedalo: A pedal-powered pleasure boat, popular on lakes and at the seaside, is not a warship, whatever the kids say.
Types of warship.Junk: The Chinese junk has battened sails and was used for trade and exploration, and huge ones sailed under Admiral Zheng He.
Types of warship.Houseboat: Houseboats are floating homes, and Kerala's famous kettuvallam are converted rice barges.
Types of warship.Cruise ship: A modern cruise ship can carry over 6,000 passengers, but it is built for leisure and is a civilian vessel.
Types of warship.Paddle steamer: A trap: some were turned into warships, like Civil War gunboats, but the type is mainly known for river and lake service.
Types of warship.Punt: A flat-bottomed boat pushed with a pole, it is famous at Oxford and Cambridge, not in a navy.
Types of warship.Narrowboat: British canal narrowboats are about 2 meters wide to fit the narrow locks, which is why they are so long and thin.
Types of warship.Swan boat: The swan boats of Boston's Public Garden have been pedaled around since 1877 by a driver hidden behind the swan.
Types of warship.Jet ski: It is a trademark of Kawasaki that came to mean any personal watercraft, and it is not a warship, though some navies use similar craft.
Types of warship.Trawler: Trawlers are fishing boats that drag a net, and during the Cod Wars of the 1970s they became sources of Icelandic-British clashes.

Things in a recording studio.Mixing desk: A mixing desk balances many recorded tracks, adjusting the volume, tone and effects of each. Big analog consoles can cost as much as a house.
Things in a recording studio.Microphone: Studio condenser mics are more sensitive than stage ones and need power, usually 48 volts called phantom power, sent down the cable.
Things in a recording studio.Pop filter: The mesh screen in front of a mic stops plosives, the bursts of air from 'p' and 'b' sounds that would thump on a recording.
Things in a recording studio.Headphones: Singers wear closed-back headphones so the backing track can't leak into the microphone and end up on the recording too.
Things in a recording studio.Soundproofing: Foam on studio walls mostly tames echo inside the room. Truly blocking outside noise needs heavy, sealed construction, a different job.
Things in a recording studio.Studio monitors: Unlike hi-fi speakers, studio monitors aim for a flat, unflattering sound, so producers hear flaws before listeners do.
Things in a recording studio.Vocal booth: A small, dead-sounding vocal booth keeps room echo off a singer's voice, so reverb can be added later to taste.
Things in a recording studio.Audio interface: This box turns a microphone's analog signal into digital data for the computer, and converts it back for your headphones.
Things in a recording studio.Mic stand: Boom stands let a mic hang over a drum kit, and a shock mount stops floor thumps from traveling up the stand into the recording.
Things in a recording studio.Amplifier: Engineers often put a mic right at a guitar amp's speaker cone, and moving it just a few inches noticeably changes the tone.
Things in a recording studio.Easel: An easel props up a painter's canvas. It's studio gear, but for an artist's studio rather than a recording one.
Things in a recording studio.Kiln: A kiln fires clay at over 1,000 degrees Celsius. It belongs in a pottery studio, not beside delicate microphones.
Things in a recording studio.Anvil: An anvil is a blacksmith's block. Hitting one is loud, which is exactly why it isn't welcome in a quiet studio.
Things in a recording studio.Hay bale: Hay bales belong on a farm. They absorb some sound, but recording studios use purpose-built foam and panels instead.
Things in a recording studio.Jury box: A jury box is the railed seating area where jurors sit in court. Courtrooms are for verdicts, not for recording music.
Things in a recording studio.Operating table: Operating tables sit in hospital theaters, where sterile surfaces matter far more than acoustics.
Things in a recording studio.Car lift: A car lift raises vehicles for mechanics. Garages are loud and echoey, which makes them poor places to record.
Things in a recording studio.Pulpit: Churches have lovely natural reverb, and some albums are recorded in them, but the pulpit itself isn't studio gear.
Things in a recording studio.Fire pole: Fire poles let firefighters drop quickly from the upper floors of a station, and have nothing to do with making records.
Things in a recording studio.Dental chair: A dental chair reclines under a bright lamp, and a drill's whine is a sound no producer wants on tape.
Things in a recording studio.Bunk bed: Bunk beds belong in dorms and cabins. A studio lounge would use a sofa, where tired musicians nap between takes.
Things in a recording studio.Slot machine: Slot machines are designed to be loud, with jingles tuned to excite players. That's casino gear, not studio gear.
Things in a recording studio.Loom: A loom weaves threads into cloth, and its rhythmic clacking would ruin any take. It belongs with weavers, not engineers.
Things in a recording studio.Hospital bed: Hospital beds crank up and down for patient care, and nothing about one helps capture or shape a sound.

Tools for cutting.Saw: Japanese pull saws cut on the pull stroke, so the blade can be thinner and make a narrower, cleaner cut than Western push saws.
Tools for cutting.Scissors: Two blades pivoting on a screw is the key trick: the cutting point slides along the edges, shearing the material instead of crushing it.
Tools for cutting.Shears: Sheep shears, tin shears and garden shears share a design that dates back over 2,000 years to the Romans' spring-loaded version.
Tools for cutting.Knife: The knife is among humanity's oldest tools; stone blades from about 2.5 million years ago were already being used to butcher animals.
Tools for cutting.Scalpel: Surgical scalpels use disposable blades, and some obsidian ones are sharper than steel, with edges only a few nanometers thick.
Tools for cutting.Axe: Stone axe heads were among the first tools to be traded over long distances in Neolithic Europe, prized for their quality.
Tools for cutting.Chisel: Woodworkers push a chisel with the hand or tap it with a mallet; its bevel is honed to a razor edge, often at around 25 degrees.
Tools for cutting.Box cutter: The snap-off blade was inspired by broken glass and chocolate bars: its Japanese inventor, Yoshio Okada, scored segments to snap off dull edges.
Tools for cutting.Tin snips: Despite the name, they cut sheet metal such as steel or aluminum; color-coded handles tell you whether they cut left, right or straight.
Tools for cutting.Bolt cutter: Long handles multiply the force through compound leverage, letting a person shear through padlock shackles and chain links with ease.
Tools for cutting.Scythe: The Grim Reaper carries one, but real scythes are balanced to sweep in an arc, and a skilled mower can cut an acre of grass in a day.
Tools for cutting.Machete: In Latin America and the Caribbean it's an everyday farm tool, used for cutting sugarcane far more often than for any adventure.
Tools for cutting.Hammer: Hammers drive and pound rather than cut; the claw on one side is for pulling nails, not slicing anything.
Tools for cutting.Screwdriver: A trap: it turns screws and doesn't cut, though its tip is sometimes misused as a pry bar or chisel.
Tools for cutting.Wrench: It grips and turns nuts and bolts; the British call most kinds a spanner. Either way, it has no blade for cutting.
Tools for cutting.Spirit level: The bubble floats in alcohol rather than water because alcohol doesn't freeze and moves smoothly; it measures flatness, not cuts.
Tools for cutting.Tape measure: Its hook at the end is deliberately loose by the hook's own thickness, so inside and outside measurements both come out right.
Tools for cutting.Mallet: A mallet is soft-faced, often of wood or rubber, so you can strike a chisel or panel without marring it; it never cuts on its own.
Tools for cutting.Trowel: Brick and plastering trowels are for spreading mortar; the small pointed garden version digs rather than cuts.
Tools for cutting.Paintbrush: Artists' "camel hair" brushes never come from camels; they're usually made from squirrel or pony hair, and the best from sable.
Tools for cutting.Stapler: Staples punch through paper and fold their legs over, but fastening isn't cutting; the stapler pins sheets together instead.
Tools for cutting.Clamp: A clamp holds work steady so you can cut it safely; the clamp itself has no edge at all.
Tools for cutting.Plunger: Its rubber cup works by pushing and pulling water in a drain, so it clears clogs by pressure and never by cutting.
Tools for cutting.Funnel: It guides liquid through a narrow opening; the word comes from the Latin infundibulum, and the tool has no cutting edge.

Programming data types.Integer: Integers are whole numbers. In many languages a 32-bit signed integer maxes out at about 2.1 billion, which has caused famous overflow bugs.
Programming data types.String: A string is a sequence of characters, like text. The word comes from characters being "strung" together in a row.
Programming data types.Boolean: Booleans hold only true or false and are named after George Boole, a 19th-century mathematician who built the algebra of logic.
Programming data types.Float: Floats store decimal numbers approximately, so 0.1 plus 0.2 doesn't exactly equal 0.3 in most languages. It's a classic programmer surprise.
Programming data types.Array: An array stores items in a numbered list, and in most languages counting starts at 0, not 1. That's a famous source of off-by-one mistakes.
Programming data types.Char: A char holds a single character such as a letter. In C it is just a small integer, so 'A' is stored as the number 65.
Programming data types.Double: A double is a double-precision floating-point number, using 64 bits to hold about 15 to 16 digits. It's twice the size of a float.
Programming data types.Tuple: A tuple is a fixed group of values. The word generalizes pair, triple, quadruple and so on, and Python writes them in parentheses.
Programming data types.List: A list holds an ordered collection of items. Python lists can mix types, so one list can contain numbers, text and other lists.
Programming data types.Dictionary: A dictionary stores key-value pairs for quick lookup, like a real one. Other languages call it a map, hash or associative array.
Programming data types.Byte: A byte is eight bits and is often used as a data type for small values from 0 to 255. It's also the standard unit of storage.
Programming data types.Pixel: A pixel is a dot in an image, and the word comes from picture element. It's a display concept rather than a data type.
Programming data types.Router: A router directs data between networks. It's hardware, not something you declare in a program.
Programming data types.Compiler: A compiler translates source code into machine code. Grace Hopper wrote an early one in 1952. It's a tool, not a type of data.
Programming data types.Browser: A browser is the program you use to view websites. It's software, not a type of data inside a program.
Programming data types.Cursor: A cursor marks your place on screen. In database programming, the word also means something else, but a cursor isn't a basic data type.
Programming data types.Widget: A widget is a user-interface element like a button or slider. It's an object, not a basic type, though the word began as a generic name for a gadget.
Programming data types.Firewall: A firewall filters network traffic. The name borrows from the barrier that stops fire spreading in buildings and cars.
Programming data types.Server: A server is a computer that provides services to other computers. It's hardware or a program, not a type of data.
Programming data types.Plugin: A plugin adds features to an existing program, like browser extensions. It's a software add-on, not a data type.
Programming data types.Cookie: A cookie is a small bit of data websites store in your browser. The name comes from earlier "magic cookie" ideas. It isn't a type in a language.
Programming data types.Folder: A folder is a way to organize files, borrowed from office stationery. It's a file-system concept, not a data type.
Programming data types.Hashtag: A hashtag is a word with the # sign in front, popularized by Twitter in 2007. It's social-media syntax, not a data type.
Programming data types.Modem: A modem turns digital signals into sounds or signals for telephone and cable lines. It's a device, not a data type.

Chinese tech companies.Huawei: Founded in Shenzhen in 1987 by Ren Zhengfei, Huawei is one of the biggest telecom equipment makers in the world.
Chinese tech companies.Xiaomi: The name is usually translated as 'millet', and the company, founded in 2010, became a leading phone maker globally.
Chinese tech companies.Lenovo: Lenovo bought IBM's PC business in 2005, including the ThinkPad line, and grew into the world's top PC maker.

Linux terminal commands.ls: Lists directory contents, and ls -la also reveals hidden files, which are the ones whose names start with a dot.
Linux terminal commands.cd: Changes directory. Typing cd alone takes you home, and cd - jumps back to the directory you were in before.
Linux terminal commands.pwd: Stands for print working directory, and it tells you exactly where you are in the file tree.
Linux terminal commands.mkdir: Makes a directory, and the -p flag builds a whole nested path of folders in one go.
Linux terminal commands.rm: Removes files with no recycle bin to rescue them, and rm -rf / is the infamous command that can wipe a whole system.
Linux terminal commands.cp: Copies files, and you need the -r flag to copy a directory with everything inside it.
Linux terminal commands.mv: Moving and renaming are the same operation in Unix, so this one command does both jobs.
Linux terminal commands.grep: The name comes from the old ed editor command g/re/p, meaning global regular expression print.
Linux terminal commands.cat: Short for concatenate, it was designed to join files together, though most people use it to view just one.
Linux terminal commands.chmod: Changes permissions; chmod 755 gives the owner full access and everyone else read and execute rights.
Linux terminal commands.sudo: Short for superuser do, it runs a single command with root privileges, and it asks for your password first.
Linux terminal commands.echo: Prints text to the terminal, and it's a staple of shell scripts for showing messages and variable values.
Linux terminal commands.touch: Its original purpose is updating a file's timestamp, but it's mostly used to create an empty file.
Linux terminal commands.cls: A trap: that's how Windows' Command Prompt clears the screen, while Linux uses clear for the same job.
Linux terminal commands.del: A DOS and Windows command for deleting files; the Linux equivalent is rm.
Linux terminal commands.makedir: Not a command anywhere. The real one is mkdir, and Windows has md as a shorter alias.
Linux terminal commands.remove: No such command exists. The Linux command is rm, and rmdir removes only empty directories.
Linux terminal commands.listdir: That's a real Python function, os.listdir, but it isn't a shell command; in a terminal ls does the job.
Linux terminal commands.move: Windows has a command called move, but Linux handles that task with mv, which also does renaming.
Linux terminal commands.delete: Not a Linux command. rm removes files, and a lesser-known unlink command also exists for the job.
Linux terminal commands.show: No command by this name exists. You'd use cat, less or more to display a file's contents.
Linux terminal commands.erase: A DOS command that works like del, so it's from the Microsoft world and not a Linux one.
Linux terminal commands.folder: Linux calls them directories, and no command named folder exists, though graphical desktops do say folder.
Linux terminal commands.list: Not a command. The tool that lists directory contents is ls, which stands for list.

On display at the Louvre.Mona Lisa: Stolen from the Louvre in 1911 by a museum worker, it was missing for two years, a theft that made it the world's most famous painting.
On display at the Louvre.Venus de Milo: Found on the Greek island of Milos in 1820, it's about 2,100 years old, and nobody agrees what its missing arms once did.
On display at the Louvre.Winged Victory: The headless Nike of Samothrace, about 2,200 years old, stands atop a grand staircase and is carved as if landing on a ship's prow.
On display at the Louvre.Raft of the Medusa: Géricault's huge 1819 painting of survivors adrift after a real shipwreck. He studied corpses from morgues for realism.
On display at the Louvre.The Lacemaker: Vermeer's painting is tiny, about 24 by 21 centimeters, with a blurred foreground thread that looks like a camera effect.
On display at the Louvre.Grande Odalisque: Ingres's 1814 nude was criticized for having extra vertebrae; her back looks impossibly long, which was deliberate.
On display at the Louvre.Oath of the Horatii: David's 1784 painting of Roman brothers swearing to fight for Rome became a defining work of neoclassicism.
On display at the Louvre.Virgin of the Rocks: Leonardo painted two versions. The Louvre owns one and London's National Gallery owns the other.
On display at the Louvre.The Seated Scribe: An Egyptian statue about 4,500 years old, whose inlaid eyes of rock crystal still look startlingly alive.
On display at the Louvre.Code of Hammurabi: A black basalt column about 3,800 years old, carved with nearly 300 laws, including the principle of "an eye for an eye".
On display at the Louvre.The Starry Night: Van Gogh painted it from his asylum room in 1889, and it hangs in New York's MoMA, not in the Louvre.
On display at the Louvre.The Night Watch: Rembrandt's giant 1642 canvas hangs in Amsterdam's Rijksmuseum. Its name came from darkened varnish, as it's actually a daytime scene.
On display at the Louvre.The Birth of Venus: Botticelli's masterpiece hangs in Florence's Uffizi Gallery, so you would have to leave Paris to see it.
On display at the Louvre.Las Meninas: Velázquez's puzzling royal portrait hangs in Madrid's Prado, and the painter himself appears in it.
On display at the Louvre.The Scream: Munch painted several versions, and the best known are held in Oslo's museums rather than in Paris.
On display at the Louvre.American Gothic: Grant Wood's 1930 farm couple hangs in the Art Institute of Chicago. His models were his dentist and sister.
On display at the Louvre.Guernica: Picasso's 1937 anti-war mural hangs in Madrid's Reina Sofía, after being kept in New York until Spain became a democracy.
On display at the Louvre.Michelangelo's David: Florence's marble David is in the city's Accademia. The Louvre holds Michelangelo's Dying Slave and Rebellious Slave instead.
On display at the Louvre.Nighthawks: Hopper's 1942 diner scene hangs in the Art Institute of Chicago, so it's an American painting in an American museum.
On display at the Louvre.Primavera: Botticelli's spring allegory also hangs in Florence's Uffizi, not the Louvre, despite its fame.
On display at the Louvre.The Kiss: Klimt's is in Vienna's Belvedere, and Rodin's marble is in Paris's Musée Rodin, not the Louvre.
On display at the Louvre.Elgin Marbles: The Parthenon sculptures are in the British Museum, where they remain the subject of a long dispute with Greece.
On display at the Louvre.Rosetta Stone: French soldiers found it in 1799, but Britain seized it after the French defeat, so it sits in the British Museum.
On display at the Louvre.Christina's World: Wyeth's 1948 painting hangs in New York's MoMA, where it is one of the museum's best-loved pictures.

Salty snacks and foods.Pretzel: Pretzels are dipped in lye before baking, which creates the dark, glossy crust that holds the coarse salt.
Salty snacks and foods.Potato chip: Smith's of England began packing a twist of salt into bags of chips in the 1920s so people could season them themselves.
Salty snacks and foods.Soy sauce: Traditional soy sauce is brewed from soybeans, wheat, salt and mold, and ferments for months before pressing.
Salty snacks and foods.Bacon: Bacon is pork belly cured in salt, often with sugar and nitrite, which is why it's both salty and long-lasting.
Salty snacks and foods.Anchovy: Anchovies are cured in salt, and they're the hidden umami in Worcestershire sauce.
Salty snacks and foods.Olive: Raw olives are bitter and inedible, and curing in brine or lye is what makes them edible and salty.
Salty snacks and foods.Feta: Feta is aged in brine, and EU law reserves the name for Greek cheese made from sheep's milk or sheep-and-goat milk.
Salty snacks and foods.Seawater: Seawater is about 3.5 percent salt, so drinking it dehydrates you: your kidneys can't make urine saltier than the sea.
Salty snacks and foods.Saltine: Saltines get their name from the sprinkle of salt on top, and the tiny holes (docking) stop them puffing up as they bake.
Salty snacks and foods.Beef jerky: Salt pulls water out of meat, which is why drying and curing together became an ancient way to preserve jerky.
Salty snacks and foods.Miso: Miso is fermented soybeans with koji mold, and the longer it ages the darker and saltier it tends to get.
Salty snacks and foods.Fish sauce: Fish sauce is anchovies fermented in salt; ancient Romans made a similar condiment called garum.
Salty snacks and foods.Capers: Capers are the flower buds of a Mediterranean shrub, pickled in salt or brine; the larger fruit are called caperberries.
Salty snacks and foods.Honey: Honey is sweet because bees dehydrate nectar, and its low water content is why it practically never spoils.
Salty snacks and foods.Watermelon: Watermelon is a trap: it's sweet, yet many people sprinkle on salt, which suppresses bitterness and makes the sweetness pop.
Salty snacks and foods.Cotton candy: Cotton candy is nearly pure sugar spun into threads, and a puff is mostly air.
Salty snacks and foods.Apple: About a quarter of an apple's volume is air, which is why apples float.
Salty snacks and foods.Strawberry: Strawberries are sweet-tart, and the seeds on the outside, called achenes, are technically the true fruits.
Salty snacks and foods.Sugar: Sugar crystals look just like salt, a classic kitchen mix-up that has ruined plenty of recipes.
Salty snacks and foods.Marshmallow: Marshmallow is sugar, gelatin and air whipped together, sweet all the way through.
Salty snacks and foods.Banana: Botanically bananas are berries, and sweet ones at that.
Salty snacks and foods.Grape: Grapes taste sweet, and raisins are simply grapes dried until their sugar concentrates.
Salty snacks and foods.Maple syrup: It takes roughly 40 gallons of maple sap, boiled down, to make a single gallon of syrup.
Salty snacks and foods.Rice pudding: Rice pudding is a sweet comfort food in many countries, even though plain rice is quite bland.

Foods that grow underground.Ginger: The ginger you eat is a rhizome, an underground stem, not a root.
Foods that grow underground.Parsnip: Parsnips turn sweeter after frost as their starch converts to sugar.
Foods that grow underground.Sweet potato: Sweet potatoes aren't related to potatoes; they belong to the morning glory family.
Foods that grow underground.Cassava: Cassava feeds hundreds of millions, but raw it contains cyanide compounds and must be processed.
Foods that grow underground.Peanut: Peanut flowers bloom above ground, then the stalk pushes the pods into the soil to ripen; peanuts are legumes.
Foods that grow underground.Tomato: A tomato grows on the vine above ground, and is botanically a fruit.
Foods that grow underground.Cucumber: Cucumbers grow on vines above ground, and are about 95 percent water.
Foods that grow underground.Broccoli: Broccoli is a cluster of flower buds eaten before they bloom, growing above ground.
Foods that grow underground.Corn: Corn grows on tall stalks above ground, and each silk strand on an ear leads to one kernel.
Foods that grow underground.Lettuce: Lettuce grows its leaves above the soil, and it's actually related to the sunflower.
Foods that grow underground.Bell pepper: Bell peppers hang above ground, and green ones are simply unripe.
Foods that grow underground.Pumpkin: Pumpkins grow on the ground as vines, and the biggest weigh well over 1,000 kilograms.

Foods that grow underground.Zucchini: Zucchini grows above ground, a summer squash whose flowers are edible.
Foods that grow underground.Eggplant: An eggplant is botanically a berry growing above ground, and it's related to tomatoes and potatoes.
Foods that grow underground.Cauliflower: Cauliflower is a flower head above ground, and it's white because leaves shield it from the sun.
Foods that grow underground.Green beans: Green beans are pods hanging on bushes or vines above ground, and are picked while the seeds are small.

Things that swell up in water.Compressed sponge: Compressed sponges are flat and hard until water makes them expand into full sponges in seconds.
Things that swell up in water.Dry pasta: Dry pasta roughly doubles in weight as it absorbs water while cooking.
Things that swell up in water.Rolled oats: Rolled oats swell as they absorb liquid, and that creates the creamy texture of porridge.
Things that swell up in water.Diaper: Diapers contain sodium polyacrylate, a super-absorbent polymer that can hold many times its weight in liquid.
Things that swell up in water.Tapioca pearls: Tapioca pearls come from cassava root starch, and they swell into chewy balls in boba tea.
Things that swell up in water.Lentils: Lentils swell as they cook, and they're one of the oldest cultivated crops, with a history of thousands of years.
Things that swell up in water.Couscous: Couscous is tiny steamed pasta from North Africa, and it swells up in just a few minutes with hot water.
Things that swell up in water.Grow-a-dinosaur toy: These toys are made of a polymer that absorbs water and expands to several times their original size over days.
Things that swell up in water.Marble: A glass marble is solid and nonporous, so water can't get in and it won't change size.
Things that swell up in water.Coin: A metal coin doesn't absorb water at all, though it may corrode over time.
Things that swell up in water.Plastic toy: Most plastic toys are waterproof, so they don't swell, and are made to survive the bath.
Things that swell up in water.Glass: Glass is nonporous and doesn't absorb water, which is why it's used for storing things.
Things that swell up in water.Rock: Most rocks barely absorb any water, though some clays swell when they get wet.
Things that swell up in water.Steel nail: A steel nail doesn't swell in water, but it will rust over time.
Things that swell up in water.Candle: Candle wax is water-repellent, and it doesn't absorb any water.
Things that swell up in water.Sugar: Sugar dissolves in water rather than swelling, and it disappears into the liquid.
Things that swell up in water.Salt: Salt dissolves in water, so it doesn't swell, and seawater is about 3.5 percent salt.
Things that swell up in water.Rubber ball: A rubber ball is non-absorbent and keeps its shape in water.
Things that swell up in water.Seashell: A seashell is made of calcium carbonate, which doesn't swell in water, though acid can dissolve it.
Things that swell up in water.Ice cube: An ice cube melts into water and shrinks, so it doesn't swell.

Things from Doctor Who.The Master: The Doctor's renegade Time Lord nemesis has been played by Roger Delgado, Anthony Ainley, John Simm, and Sacha Dhawan, and Michelle Gomez as Missy.
Things from Doctor Who.Davros: Creator of the Daleks, who sits in a Dalek-like chair, with a creator-of-evil backstory first told in 1975.
Things from Doctor Who.Sontaran: Squat, clone-born militarists who are warlike and have a weak spot at the back of their necks; Strax is a Sontaran nurse.
Things from Doctor Who.K-9: The Doctor's robot dog companion, voiced by John Leeson, who got his own spinoff series.
Things from Doctor Who.Ood: Tentacle-faced, telepathic servants carrying their brains in their hands, introduced in 2006.
Things from Doctor Who.Lightsaber: Star Wars' glowing energy sword belongs to Jedi and Sith; it has nothing to do with the TARDIS or Time Lords.
Things from Doctor Who.Phaser: Star Trek's standard stun-or-kill handheld weapon, not from Doctor Who.
Things from Doctor Who.Tricorder: Star Trek's scanning gadget, which scans the surroundings; the Doctor uses a sonic screwdriver instead.
Things from Doctor Who.Warp drive: Star Trek's faster-than-light engine, invented by Zefram Cochrane, unlike the TARDIS.
Things from Doctor Who.DeLorean: The time machine from Back to the Future is the 1980s car that reaches 88 miles per hour.
Things from Doctor Who.Flux capacitor: The Back to the Future device that makes time travel possible, needing 1.21 gigawatts.
Things from Doctor Who.Borg: Star Trek's cyborg collective, to which Cybermen are often compared, but they are a different franchise.
Things from Doctor Who.Klingon: Star Trek's warrior race, with their own invented language, not Doctor Who's.
Things from Doctor Who.Hoverboard: Marty McFly's floating skateboard from Back to the Future Part II, set in 2015.
Things from Doctor Who.Death Star: Star Wars' moon-sized superweapon, which can destroy planets.
Things from Doctor Who.Jedi: Star Wars' Force-wielding order, not Time Lords.
Things from Doctor Who.Holodeck: Star Trek's virtual reality room, with a famous safety-protocol-failures plot.
